Ratio prioris est: quia subjicibile, qua tale, non est praedicabile, ut per se constat; ergo cum Logicum sit Universale praedicabile, subjicibile, qua tale, non erit universale Logicum. Atqui cum universale metaphysicum nec in praedicabilitate, nec in subjicibilitate situm sit; sed in inexistentia unius in multis, sicut subjicibile, qua tale, potest adhuc esse unum aptum esse in multis, ita etiam poterit esse universale metaphysicum. Ratio posterioris est, quia Genus, quod est subjicibile, (verbi gratia animal respectu viventis,) est etiam praedicabile respectu rationalis, & irrationalis.

VII. Q. *An Genus in communi, univoce predicetur de Genere entis realis, & entis rationis?* Respondeo. Haec duo Genera secundum suas partes materiales tantum convenire inter se analogice; quia Ens tantum analogice potest praedicari de ente reali, & ente rationis. At vero si in esse generis, & prout sunt considerationis Logicae accipiantur; cum utriusque idem prorsus sit artificium Logicum, & conceptus, dubium non esse, quia univoce inter se conveniant.

VIII. Q. *Cum Genus summum ab infimo aeque multum distet, quam Genus infimum a Specie; cur Genus infimum aliud est universale, quam species; & Genus summum non aliud, quam genus infimum?* Respondeo. Diversitatem istam non petendam esse a majori vel minori distantia, quam universalia habent in linea praedicamentali; sed ab eorum conceptu quidditativo. Cum itaque & Genus summum, & Genus infimum praedicentur ut pars materialis; species vero, ut tota essentia; dubium esse nullum potest, quin species a Genere infimo plus differat, quam hoc a summo.

IX. Q. *An conceptus definiens Genus signatum sit conceptus faciens formaliter Genus exercitum?* Respondeo. Cum conceptus faciens Genus in actu exercito debeat etiam facere universale in actu exercito; universale autem fieri non possit per conceptum simplicem non abstrahentem a multitudine; & conceptus definiens Genus signatum non abstrahat a multitudine; sicut est conceptus simplex, ita non est conceptus faciens Genus in actu exercito. Per definitionem itaque Generis definitur Genus signate, non autem fit exercite.

X. Q. *Quid sit species in communi sumpta?* Respondeo. Etsi certum sit, speciem metaphysicam sumptam in communi recte posse dici, *Unum aptum inesse multis ut tota essentia*; ingens tamen inter hanc & speciem Logicam cum sit discrimen, non immerito quaeri posset, an cum Logicum universale sit praedicabile, Speciei Logicae dari possit definitio in communi? Hinc de hac definitione apud autores altum ubique silentium, semper definientes speciem vel praedicabilem tantum, vel tantum subjicibilem. Censemus itaque Speciei in communi sumptae, prout includit Praedicabilem, & subjicibilem, non posse aliam meliorem hac (*Unum aptum ut totam essentiam terminare propositionem*,) definitionem dari. Nolumus tamen asserere, alios male egisse, dum speciem prius diviserunt, & divisam primum definierunt. Nam

The reason for the former is: because subjectible [as such], as such, is not predicable, as is clear in itself; therefore, since a Logical [Universal] is a predicable universal, subjectible as such will not be a logical universal. But since a metaphysical universal is situated neither in predicability nor in subjectibility, but in the inexistence of one in many, just as subjectible as such can still be one apt to be in many, so also it will be able to be a metaphysical universal. The reason for the latter is because a Genus that is subjectible (for example animal with respect to living) is also predicable with respect to rational and irrational.

VII. Question. *Is Genus in common predicated univocally of the Genus of real being and of being of reason?* I answer. These two Genera agree among themselves analogically only according to their material parts; because Being can only be predicated analogically of real being and of being of reason. But if they are taken in the being of genus, and as they are of logical consideration, since the logical artifice and concept of both is absolutely the same, there is no doubt that they agree among themselves univocally.

VIII. Question. *Since the highest Genus is as far removed from the lowest as the lowest Genus is from the Species; why is the lowest Genus a different universal than the species; and the highest Genus not different from the lowest genus?* I answer. This diversity is not to be sought from the greater or lesser distance that universals have in the predicamental line; but from their quidditative concept. Since, therefore, both the highest Genus and the lowest Genus are predicated as a material part; the species, however, as the whole essence; there can be no doubt that the species differs more from the lowest Genus than this does from the highest.

IX. Question. *Is the concept defining the signed Genus the concept making the exercised Genus?* I answer. Since the concept making a Genus in the exercised act <note>original: "in actu exercito"</note> must also make a universal in the exercised act; but a universal cannot be created by a simple concept not abstracting from a multitude; and the concept defining the signed Genus <note>original: "Genus signatum"</note> does not abstract from a multitude, as it is a simple concept, so it is not a concept making Genus in the exercised act. Therefore, by the definition of Genus, Genus is defined in the signed way, but it is not created in the exercised way.

X. Question. *What is species taken in common?* I answer. Although it is certain that a metaphysical species taken in common can rightly be called, *One apt to be in many as the whole essence*; nevertheless, since there is a great difference between this and a Logical species, it could not unfairly be asked whether, since a Logical universal is predicable, a definition in common can be given to a Logical Species? Hence, there is everywhere a deep silence among authors regarding this definition, always defining species either as only predicable, or as only subjectible. We think, therefore, that for a Species taken in common, as it includes the Predicable and the subjectible, no better definition can be given than this: (*One apt to terminate a proposition as the whole essence*). It is written, "For those who know Your name will trust in You." And it is written, "As for me, may my prayer be to You, O Lord, at a favorable time." Now, a "favorable time" is the revelation of the Supreme Will. The revelation of this Will is the aspect of the expansion of light. The expansion of light is the revelation of Divinity. The revelation of Divinity is the expansion of Wisdom. The expansion of Wisdom is the revelation of Understanding. The revelation of Understanding is the expansion of Loving-kindness. The expansion of Loving-kindness is the revelation of Might. The revelation of Might is the expansion of Splendor. The expansion of Splendor is the revelation of Victory. The revelation of Victory is the expansion of Glory. The expansion of Glory is the revelation of Foundation. The revelation of Foundation is the expansion of Kingdom. The expansion of Kingdom is the revelation of the Divine Presence. The revelation of the Divine Presence is the aspect of the expansion of light. The expansion of light is the revelation of Divinity. The revelation of Divinity is the expansion of Wisdom. The expansion of Wisdom is the revelation of Understanding. The revelation of Understanding is the expansion of Loving-kindness. The expansion of Loving-kindness is the revelation of Might. The revelation of Might is the expansion of Splendor. The expansion of Splendor is the revelation of Victory. The revelation of Victory is the expansion of Glory. The expansion of Glory is the revelation of Foundation. The revelation of Foundation is the expansion of Kingdom. The expansion of Kingdom is the revelation of the Divine Presence.

Mendaciunculum, plusculum. Sin minus rite formentur, diminutiua non sunt. Auunculus, Cuniculus, Musculus, quando non est paruus mus, Pediculus, uel (ut alij uolunt) pedunculus: et penultima longa cuculus. Cicercula nomen leguminis. Nouacula culter rasorius. Lenticula uasculi genus: alia masculina, aut foeminina non occurrunt. Seruius tamen super Donatum ait. acus acicula. Acus enim dicitur, qua uestes sarciuntur. Acicula, qua mulieres utuntur ad ornamentum capitis. Adiectiua tria, Anniculus, Ridiculus, uernaculus: anniculus puer, annicula puella, anniculum iumentum, hoc est unius anni: sicut Bimus, ma, mum, id est duorum annorum. Trimus, trima, trimum, id est trium annorum. Quadrimus, quadrima, quadrimum, id est quatuor annorum, et non amplius: nec de animalibus modo, sed de inanimatis, ut anniculum uinum, bimum oleum. De pueris tamen magis loquimur per diminutionem, bimulus, trimulus, quadrimulus, quia intra hos annos adhuc parui sunt. Similiter de his, in quibus haec ratio habet locum, ut anniculus equus, bimus aries, trimus porcus, quadrimum uinum, bimulus puer, trimula puella. Dissimiliter in quibus haec ratio locum non habet. Ridiculus homo, ridicula res, ridiculum caput, id est deridendum. Est etiam saepe neutrum, significatque plerunque sermonem risus potius, quam derisus excitantem. uernaculus, uernacula, uernaculum, quod est domi nostrae, uel in nostra patria natum, ut lingua uernacula, quod uulgo dicunt lingua materna: dictum est a uerna, qui est seruus domi nostrae natus, id est ex nostra ancilla. Praeterea neutra multa sunt, ut, umbraculum, Tabernaculum, spectaculum, Habitaculum, Coenaculum, Crepusculum, Germiculum pro germine, Crepitaculum, Vinculum, Amiculum pro amictus genere quodam fere pallio. Curriculum pro cursu, et pro loco, in quo certamen currendi exercetur, nonnunquam etiam pro curru, ut Curtius libro octauo. Aliorum turbati equi non in uoragines modo, lacunasque, sed etiam in amnem praecipitauere curricula. Cubiculum, quod certe a cubili non uenit, quum intra cubiculum cubile sit, et eius diminutiuum foret cubicululum. Puluis et significatione, et formatione legitima diminutiuum facit, sed genus mutat apud Hieronymum, ut uile puluisculum: masculine tamen posuit Apuleius in quodam suo carmine, de quo meminit in apologia de Magia. Misi (ut petisti) munditias dentium, nitelas oris, Ex Arabicis frugibus tenuem, candidicum, nobilem puluisculum, Complanatorem tumidulae gingiulae, sarritorem pridianae reliquiae, Ne qua uisatur tetra labes sordium, Restrictis si forte labellis riseris. Conuentus quoque facit conuenticulum.

translation:
### Concerning diminutive nouns. Chapter V.

Diminutive nouns ending in such a sound as *pisciculus* <gloss>little fish</gloss>, if they are rightly formed, are true diminutives, such as *Pisciculus*, *vermiculus* <gloss>little worm</gloss>, *Passerculus* <gloss>little sparrow</gloss>, *Fraterculus* <gloss>little brother</gloss>, *Securicula* <gloss>little axe</gloss>, *Lucubratiuncula* <gloss>short period of work by candlelight</gloss>, *virguncula* <gloss>little maiden</gloss>, *Sororcula* <gloss>little sister</gloss>, *Munusculum* <gloss>little gift</gloss>, *Corpusculum* <gloss>little body</gloss>, *Mendaciunculum* <gloss>little lie</gloss>, *plusculum* <gloss>a little more</gloss>. If they are not rightly formed, they are not diminutives. *Auunculus* <gloss>uncle</gloss>, *Cuniculus* <gloss>rabbit/mine</gloss>, *Musculus* <gloss>muscle</gloss> (when it is not a small mouse), *Pediculus* <gloss>louse</gloss>, or (as others wish) *pedunculus* <gloss>peduncle</gloss>: and with a long penult, *cuculus* <gloss>cuckoo</gloss>. *Cicercula* <gloss>vetch</gloss> is the name of a legume. *Nouacula* <gloss>razor</gloss> is a shaving knife. *Lenticula* <gloss>lentil/small vessel</gloss> is a kind of small vessel: other masculine or feminine nouns do not occur. Servius, however, on Donatus says: *acus* <gloss>needle</gloss>, *acicula* <gloss>little needle/pin</gloss>. For *acus* is said of that which is used to mend clothes. *Acicula* is what women use for the ornament of the hair. Three adjectives: *Anniculus* <gloss>one year old</gloss>, *Ridiculus* <gloss>ridiculous</gloss>, *uernaculus* <gloss>vernacular/native</gloss>; *anniculus puer* <gloss>a boy of one year</gloss>, *annicula puella* <gloss>a girl of one year</gloss>, *anniculum iumentum* <gloss>a beast of one year</gloss>, that is, of one year: just as *Bimus, -ma, -mum*, that is, of two years. *Trimus, -ma, -mum*, that is, of three years. *Quadrimus, -ma, -mum*, that is, of four years, and no more: and this not only of animals, but of inanimate things, as *anniculum uinum* <gloss>one-year-old wine</gloss>, *bimum oleum* <gloss>two-year-old oil</gloss>. We speak of children, however, more through diminution: *bimulus*, *trimulus*, *quadrimulus*, because within these years they are still small. Similarly for those in which this reasoning holds place, such as *anniculus equus* <gloss>one-year-old horse</gloss>, *bimus aries* <gloss>two-year-old ram</gloss>, *trimus porcus* <gloss>three-year-old pig</gloss>, *quadrimum uinum* <gloss>four-year-old wine</gloss>, *bimulus puer* <gloss>young two-year-old boy</gloss>, *trimula puella* <gloss>young three-year-old girl</gloss>. Dissimilarly in those in which this reasoning has no place. *Ridiculus homo* <gloss>a ridiculous man</gloss>, *ridicula res* <gloss>a ridiculous thing</gloss>, *ridiculum caput* <gloss>a ridiculous person</gloss>, that is, to be laughed at. It is also often neuter, and generally signifies speech exciting laughter rather than ridicule. *Vernaculus, -la, -lum* is that which is born in our house or in our native land, such as *lingua uernacula* <gloss>vernacular language</gloss>, which common people call the mother tongue: it is said from *uerna*, which is a slave born in our house, that is, from our maid. Furthermore, there are many neuters, such as *umbraculum* <gloss>shady place</gloss>, *Tabernaculum* <gloss>tent</gloss>, *spectaculum* <gloss>spectacle</gloss>, *Habitaculum* <gloss>dwelling</gloss>, *Coenaculum* <gloss>dining room</gloss>, *Crepusculum* <gloss>twilight</gloss>, *Germiculum* for *germen* <gloss>bud</gloss>, *Crepitaculum* <gloss>rattle</gloss>, *Vinculum* <gloss>bond/chain</gloss>, *Amiculum* for a kind of clothing or garment, almost a cloak. *Curriculum* <gloss>course/running track</gloss> for a course, and for the place in which the competition of running is exercised, and sometimes also for a chariot, as Curtius in the eighth book: *The horses were thrown into confusion, casting them down not only into pits and marshes but even into the river’s courses <term>curricula</term>.* *Cubiculum* <gloss>bedroom</gloss>, which certainly does not come from *cubile* <gloss>bed</gloss>, since within a *cubiculum* there is a *cubile*, and its diminutive would be *cubicululum*. *Puluis* <gloss>dust</gloss> forms a diminutive both in meaning and in legitimate formation, but it changes gender according to Jerome, as *uile puluisculum* <gloss>vile little dust</gloss>: Apuleius, however, placed it in the masculine in one of his poems, of which he makes mention in his *Apology on Magic*: *I sent (as you asked) the refinements of teeth, the glosses of the mouth, / From Arabian fruits a thin, white, noble little dust <term>puluisculum</term>, / The smoother of the swollen gum, the weeder of yesterday's remains, / So that no foul stain of filth may be seen, / If by chance you smile with tightened lips.* *Conuentus* <gloss>assembly</gloss> also forms *conuenticulum* <gloss>little meeting place</gloss>.

possit formam accipere res magisterii. Postquam ergo primo gradu soluimus; secundo coagulamus, ibi humiditate dominante, hic siccitate. Ita qui in cæteris quoque artificiis per digestionem in balneo aut fimo foluerunt separantque essentias, postquam repurgarunt, & exaltarunt lingulas, eas vniunt vicissim calore sicco, quem cineribus tribuunt. Quo circa Lullii clausicula calorem balnei & cinerum in lapidis Philosophici præparatione, nempe solutoria & coagulatoria expresse nominat.

Tertius modus ignis calidus ficcus secundo æquiparatur calori clibani, qui relinquitur extracto pane, diciturque citra combustionem leniter fundere. Hic modus plerumq; addicitur secundæ parti operis: lam enim aliquatenus affueuit igni lapis. Itaq; non amplius calor humidus requiritur. Veruntamen attendendum est, quod etiam in aliis locum habent sicubi fusio postulatur, nempe non violenta, sed blanda.

Quartus fundit simul & figit, nimirum & ipse in gradu secundo, sed moræ longioris. Quod enim prius est fusum (exemplo fit alumen, vel atramentum, vel nitrum) id perseuerante igne eodem figitur. Hinc post imbibitionem lapidis cum coagulando pergimus, tandem figimus spiritus, eodem quidem gradu, sed tamen variato secundum principium, medium, finem.

Quintus modus est calidi ficei gradu tertio, cuius effectum extra fusionem calcinare. Res enim quæ hoc igni tractatur, iam fixa est, quodammodo, nec debet fundi, sed sensim exiccari inque calcem redigi. Intelligunt tamen Philosophi non semper actualem calcis effectionem, sed talem laborem igneinque, quali alias calcinatur plumbum, lapis vel similia. Itaque & calx vocatur tunc lapis, licet lacis plebeiæ nullam formam habeat. Aurum & argentum, funderet ille modus: sed non lapidem. Furnus ei calcinatorius addicitur, cum res possit fieri in eodem vase.

Sextus quarto caloris & siccitatis gradu definitur, perhibeturque violenter fundere seu fortiter. hic scire conuenit tertio gradu perseuerante, & debite applicato, paulatim absorberi humiditatem, ita vt nulla fiat fusio: sed hic modus calcem isto modo factam dissoluit fortitudine caloris. Finge stibium paulatim absque liquefactione in calcem esse redactum gradu tertio. Ea calx quarti superuenti funditur, vt vitrefcat. In lapide fixionem solemus experiri tali igni; licet nulla fusio adesset. Sed mystica est ista liquefactio. Simul enim cum fixione & constantia in igni intelligitur.

Igni follium, quem septimum numerant, itidem violente fundimus, proflamus, separamus. Itaq; non erit gradu inferiore. Eo nonnunquam flores antimonii facimus. Alias excoquuntur isto metalla, Potest idem etiam reuerberare, calcinareque. In fortibus spiritibus proflandis eius locum sustinet per ostia & spiracula ventus subiens, vti & in vitrariis officinis.

Octauus parumi differt à septimo. Procedit faltem eius operatio per fusionem ad calcem.

Nonus dicitur in examinibus adhiberi, vt constet de fixione & cæteris argumentis bonitatis. In magisterio igitur lapidis cum aurum iam factum iudicio & examinibus subiiciendum est, iste modus vsurpatur, sed non solus. Adiiciuntur enim medicamina, vt aquæ causticæ, plumbum, sales, sulphur, stibium & reliqua de quibus apud Geberum.

Alii scriptores quatuor ignium genera commemorant, nempe Naturale, non naturale, contra naturale & elementare. Ignem naturæ vocant internum & connatum rebus: Non naturalem (quomodo Medici appellant res non naturales) ministrantem seruilemque & externum dicunt, qui occasione rei gerendæ variè administratur, vt ad putrefaciendum per balneum in prima operis parte, sed pet cineres in secunda. Ignis contra naturam violente tentat, examinatque materiam, vt iudicium fit de fixione. Eft idem etiam mysticus, nuncupaturq; Draco violentus qui comburit vt ignis inferni. Ex Mercuriali menstruo iste præparatur, eftq; intra virtrum & comburit efficacius, quam ignis elementalis seu is, qui lignis procuratur, & flammeus dicitur. Audies interdum coagulationem & dealbationem fieri calore temperatissimo, seu artificialiter attemperato, vt actus speratus existat. Sane artifex constantia caloris, & accommodatione industria, licet fit gradus primi, vel secundi, tamen assequi effectum tertii potest. Neque enim festinandum est & præcipitandus ignis, si velis per eum scienter & perite. Calcinare potes testas ouorú igni violento. Sed fi industrie agas idem assequeris etiam calore paruo interuenta aceti. Et sciendum in arte illa abstrusa intus esse menstruum potenter agens. Si importune velis operari, & ita in arte calcinare, ficut vulgus facit calcem viuam: euenerit tibi, quod lateariis, qui nimio igne perurunt lateres, & colliquant ita vt vitro fint fimiles. Itaque bene monet quidam à violento calore, & subito frigore abstinendum esse, & moderato tendum igni (ex atte per suos modos adhibito) ne incurramus in vitrificationem. Lentissimus ignis in principio soluit & separat (vt est in tractatu Petri de Zyleto) isque comparatur foliis in ariete calori, item verno, Gallinæ ouis incubantis, Embryonis: quidam per balneum administrarunt: alii per stipulas, aut cinerem, aut candelas, aut carbones &c. Omnino inciendum alieni est, eique diu insistendum, postea per gradus procedendum, quos experientia comprobar. (Igniun scientia est munus vniuersale doctrinæ) Idem ignis lenis nigritiem producit. Nihil est, quod æque extrahit humiditatem ex corporibus, & conferuat, ac ignis lenis, quia ignis attenuat naturas & liquidum à turbido sequeftrat. Lenis ignis est, quo magnesia (Mercurius Philosophorum) non refugit. Vila albedine fixio succeffit. Itaque calor augeatur, vt fimilis fiat æstiue vel leonis, & continuetur, donec massa ita calcem fathifcat, fiatque instar cineris combusti valde. Si hinc pergere cupis ad rubeum, ignem augete debes, cumque hic color apparet, tum demum forti locus est, qui alias fuforius dicitur. Intus operatur ignis argéti uiui, qui in auro & argento eam vim exercet, quæ nullo externo igni potest obtineri. Comburit enim & calcinat ea longe potentius. Sed non eft opus pluribus. Volumus hoc exemplum propofitu esse Chymico tyroni, ne putet, in hac arte temere admouendos esse ignes. Omnino affuescendum est circumspecto regimini, nec festinandum, sicubi res non requirit. Alioquin certum est detrimentum. Hoc cum non attendant illi, qui forinfecus in artem irrumpunt, putantq; se posse quoduis quouis igni

the matter of the masterwork might be able to receive form. Therefore, after we dissolve in the first grade, we coagulate in the second, with humidity dominating in the former and dryness in the latter. Thus, those who have also dissolved and separated essences in other arts through digestion in a bath or manure, after they have purified and exalted them, unite them in turn with dry heat, which they attribute to ashes. For this reason, Lull’s <note>referring to Ramon Llull, the Majorcan philosopher and alchemist</note> short clause expressly names the heat of the bath and ashes in the preparation of the Philosopher’s Stone, namely, the dissolving and coagulating heat.

The third mode of fire, warm and dry in the second grade, is equated to the heat of an oven that is left after the bread is extracted, and it is said to melt gently without combustion. This mode is mostly assigned to the second part of the work, for the stone has now become accustomed to fire to some extent. Therefore, moist heat is no longer required. However, it must be noted that it also has a place in other areas where fusion is requested, namely not violent, but mild.

The fourth melts and fixes at the same time, namely itself in the second grade, but of a longer duration. For that which has been melted first (for example, alum, or vitriol, or saltpeter) is fixed by the same fire persisting. Hence, after the imbibition of the stone, as we proceed with coagulating, we finally fix the spirits, indeed in the same grade, but varied according to the beginning, middle, and end.

The fifth mode is that of warm, dry heat in the third grade, the effect of which is to calcine, apart from fusion. For the thing treated with this fire is already fixed in a way, and ought not to be melted, but slowly dried and reduced to <term>calx</term> <gloss>powdered oxide</gloss>. The Philosophers, however, do not always mean the actual creation of lime, but such labor and fire as that by which lead, stone, or similar things are otherwise calcined. Thus, the stone is then also called lime, although it has no form of common lime. That mode would melt gold and silver, but not the stone. A calcining furnace is assigned to it, since the thing can be done in the same vessel.

The sixth is defined by the fourth grade of heat and dryness, and is said to melt violently or strongly. Here it is fitting to know that with the third grade persisting and being duly applied, the humidity is gradually absorbed so that no fusion occurs: but this mode dissolves the lime made in that way by the strength of heat. Imagine antimony gradually reduced to lime without liquefaction in the third grade. That lime is melted by the incoming fourth, so that it vitrifies. In the stone, we are accustomed to test fixation with such fire, even if no fusion were present. But that liquefaction is mystical. For it is understood together with fixation and constancy in fire.

By the fire of the bellows, which they number the seventh, we likewise melt violently, blow, and separate. Thus, it will not be of a lower grade. With it, we sometimes make flowers of antimony. Otherwise, metals are smelted by it. The same can also reverberate and calcine. In blowing strong spirits, the wind entering through the openings and vents takes its place, as also in glassworks.

The eighth differs little from the seventh. Its operation proceeds at least through fusion to lime.

The ninth is said to be used in examinations, so that it is certain regarding fixation and other proofs of quality. Therefore, in the masterwork of the stone, when the gold that has already been made must be subjected to judgment and examinations, this mode is used, but not alone. For medicinal substances are added, such as caustic waters, lead, salts, sulfur, antimony, and the rest of which one reads in Geber.

Other writers commemorate four types of fires, namely Natural, Non-natural, Contra-natural, and Elemental. They call the fire of nature internal and innate to things. They call the Non-natural (as physicians call non-natural things) serving, servile, and external, which is administered in various ways as the occasion of the task requires, such as for putrefaction through the bath in the first part of the work, but through ashes in the second. The Contra-natural fire tries and examines the matter violently, so that a judgment may be made regarding fixation. It is also mystical, and is named the violent Dragon, which burns like the fire of hell. This is prepared from Mercurial menstruum <note>a solvent or acid used in alchemy</note>, and it is inside the glass and burns more effectively than elemental fire, or that which is procured by wood and is called flaming. You will hear sometimes that coagulation and whitening are done with the most temperate heat, or artificially tempered, so that the hoped-for act may exist. Truly, the artist, by the constancy of heat and the accommodation of industry, even if it is of the first or second grade, can achieve the effect of the third. For one must not be in a hurry and the fire must not be precipitated if you wish to act knowingly and skillfully. You can calcine eggshells with violent fire. But if you act skillfully, you will achieve the same even with low heat and the intervention of vinegar. And it must be known that in that abstruse art, there is a powerfully acting menstruum within. If you wish to work importunely, and thus calcine in the art, as the common people make quicklime, it will happen to you as it does to brickmakers, who burn bricks with excessive fire and melt them so that they are like glass. Therefore, someone rightly warns that one must abstain from violent heat and sudden cold, and should tend to a moderate fire (applied from the art through its own modes), lest we incur vitrification. The slowest fire in the beginning dissolves and separates (as it is in the treatise of Peter of Zyleto), and that is compared to the heat of the ram, likewise the vernal heat, that of the hen incubating eggs, and the embryo: some have administered it through the bath: others through straw, or ash, or candles, or coals, etc. Altogether, one must begin with that which is foreign, and insist upon it for a long time, then proceed through the grades which experience confirms. (The knowledge of fires is the universal gift of doctrine). The same gentle fire produces blackness. There is nothing that extracts humidity from bodies and preserves it as well as a gentle fire, because fire attenuates natures and separates the liquid from the turbid. A gentle fire is that which magnesia (the Mercury of the Philosophers) does not flee. With whiteness, fixation succeeds. Thus, the heat should be increased so that it becomes similar to summer or lion-like heat, and continued until the mass turns into lime and becomes like burned ash. If you wish to proceed from here to red, you ought to increase the fire, and when this color appears, then at last there is a place for the strong one, which is otherwise called the fusing one. Inside, the fire of quicksilver works, which exerts in gold and silver that force which can be obtained by no external fire. For it burns and calcines them far more potently. But there is no need for more words. We want this example to be proposed to the Chemical novice, lest he think that fires are to be applied rashly in this art. One must absolutely accustom oneself to circumspect control, and not hurry, where the matter does not require it. Otherwise, harm is certain. When those who break into the art from the outside do not attend to this, they think they can do anything, anywhere.

14. Aliis placet *sensus Verborum Politicus, vel Oeconomicus, quod Adamus in hac Onomathesia virilem autoritatem, et potestatem, in uxorem ostendere voluerit, nimirum quod maritalis sit dignitatis, vel autoritatis, facultatis, vel potestatis, juris, et regiminis, Uxori nomen imponere, cum alias Uxores in Maritorum Nomen, et Familiam, potestatem, atque dominationem transeant, non contra. Verum Adamus hic nihil de sua vel dignitate, vel autoritate, nihil de jure, vel potestate, nihil de regimine, vel dominio, cogitabat, neque sua, sed ea, quae per divinam informationem audiverat, cogitabat, non suam, sed Messiae gloriam spectabat, et majora, meliora, sublimiora, sicut edoctus erat, resonabat. Qualis fuerat Dei sermo, talis etiam Adami dicitur Echo. Vitam spiritualem Deus sonabat, et Spiritus Sanctus eidem insonabat, Vitam spiritualem etiam Adami lingua resonabat.*

15. His igitur praesuppositis, nunc Compendium Adami Theologicum clarius conspicimus: tum quia *Vita spiritualis*, et *caelestis* est finis omnium articulorum fidei, vel Dogmatum Theologiae, cum *fidei finis sit salus, seu vera vita*: 1. Petri I. 9. tum quia Vita Spiritualis est *nucleus*, circa quem servandum, et ad usum applicandum, tota Theologia versatur: tum quia *Vita spiritualis* est centrum universae Theologiae, dum omnes lineae *Doctrinales* Theologiae partium ex hoc centro fluunt, et ad illud unice respiciunt: tum quia *vita spiritualis, vita mystica* Theologiae, per quam omnia capita Theologica vere vivificantur: est *anima Theologiae*, per quam omnes Theologiae partes nobis animantur.

translation:
Animal life turned toward reason, which is the mother of the living, that is, of good works, or of rightly performed deeds, to which are contrary those sins which are called dead. Truly, these things are sought from afar, nor did the Holy Spirit wish for Adam to proceed here in a disorderly manner, or to invert the order: for the life of good works necessarily presupposes, and requires before it, the life of faith, or the life in the Messiah; however, this spiritual life, founded in the Messiah, brings about both pages here in the context. Briefly, this explanation concerning moral life looks not to the sense, but to the use, not to the immediate and proximate explanation, but to the mediate and remote application.

14. To others, the political or economic sense of the words is pleasing, that Adam in this naming wished to show manly authority and power over his wife, namely that it is a matter of marital dignity, or authority, faculty, or power, right, and governance, to impose a name upon a wife, whereas otherwise wives pass into the name, family, power, and dominion of husbands, not the contrary. But Adam thought nothing here of his own dignity or authority, nothing of right or power, nothing of governance or dominion, and he did not ponder his own things, but those which he had heard through divine information; he was not looking to his own glory, but to the glory of the Messiah, and he was echoing greater, better, and more sublime things, just as he had been taught. Such as the Word of God had been, such also is the Echo of Adam said to be. God sounded forth spiritual life, and the Holy Spirit sounded it into him; the tongue of Adam also echoed forth spiritual life.

15. With these things therefore presupposed, we now see the Theological Compendium of Adam more clearly: both because spiritual and heavenly life is the end of all articles of faith, or dogmas of theology, since the end of faith is salvation, or true life (1 Peter 1:9); and because spiritual life is the nucleus around which all theology revolves, to be preserved and applied to use; and because spiritual life is the center of universal theology, while all the doctrinal lines of the parts of theology flow from this center and look solely to it; and because spiritual life, the mystical life of theology, through which all theological chapters are truly vivified, is the soul of theology, through which all parts of theology are animated for us.

## Adfinia & contraria tractans.

§. 1. Ne prolixam hic, instituamus enumerationem illarum dilationum, quae passim per omne jus diffusae, non nisi remotiorem cum nostris induciis proximitatem habent, istas tantum hic proponemus, quae propiori adfinitate nostris conjunctae sunt Induciis. Inter has autem familiam ducunt *Induciae vel à Majestate* mediante Rescripto, vel à Magistratu inferiori, eaque sive ex Legum praescripto, sive mero arbitrio concessae; quas publicas dicimus vide §. 2. translation:
# TITULUS IV.
## Treating of affinities & contraries.

§. 1. Lest we institute here a verbose enumeration of those delays <term>dilationes</term> <gloss>deferrals/delays</gloss>, which are scattered everywhere through the whole of law and have only a remote proximity to our own stays <term>induciae</term> <gloss>judicial delays/moratoriums</gloss>, we shall propose here only those which are joined to our own stays by a closer affinity. Among these, the first place is held by the *Stays either by Majesty* <note>referring to royal or sovereign authority</note> through a Rescript, or by an inferior Magistrate, and granted either by the prescription of the Laws or by mere discretion; these we call public, see §. 2. Title I. above.

§. 2. But there is also another kind of Stays, which from the form of their issuance are properly called *Letters of Security* <term>Literae Securitatis</term> <gloss>letters of protection</gloss>, and are granted by Majesty to a debtor for a three-month, six-month, annual, or other period, solely for the security of his body, so that he may not be compelled to go to prison. Yet while such a delay is current, it is nevertheless permitted for creditors to summon the debtor and to execute a judgment upon his assets, and concerning these stays see *Kinschotius’s singular treatise on the security of the body, throughout.* To these is added another kind of Stays, which are properly called *Letters of Status and Justice* <term>literas Status & Justitii</term> <gloss>letters of legal protection for those absent</gloss>, which are granted by Majesty to those who are absent for the sake of the Republic, to the end that their lawsuits might remain in the same state in which they were at the time of their departure, see *Kinschotius in the final chapter of his treatise. Rebuffus in the chapter of the treatise, in Glossary 1. Authentica 1. number 1. & Glossary 2. with those following to the end of the treatise. Fabri Codex, book 1, law 10, definition 22. 23.*

§. 3. Now as regards *Contraries*, since most things which are opposed to these Stays have been related in the previous pages, let us consider all those things which are repugnant to what we have said as contraries, *by the argument of the beginning of the Institutes on those who are their own or another's master, and Aristotle’s 1st Book of Topics 24. Others have also treated these matters broadly, after others, explicitly Freund in the chapter of the treatise, conclusion 67. & 68. Mavricius in the final chapter of the chapter of the treatise, throughout.* Lest we seem to be doing what is already done, or writing an Iliad <note>a proverbial expression meaning to write something unnecessarily long or redundant</note>, we deliberately omit those things here, ending in the name of Him with whom we began.

->BY GOD INHUMANATE!<-

translation:
<meta>continues from previous page: the mansions belonging to them due to the variety of their fruitful results.</meta>

They are called <term>vimānāni</term> <gloss>mansions</gloss> because they are characterized by distinct dimensions such as one <term>yojana</term> <gloss>a measure of distance, roughly 7-9 miles</gloss> or two <term>yojanas</term>, they shine with various jewels, have diverse colors and shapes, and through the attainment of superior splendor, they are specifically the abode of dignity. The word <term>vatthu</term> <gloss>cause or origin</gloss> means the reason for these; thus, <term>Vimānavatthu</term> <gloss>Stories of the Mansions</gloss>. The teaching that proceeds by way of such phrases as "Your seat is golden," is merely an illustration.

It should be understood as <term>Vimānavatthu</term> because this teaching occurs in dependence upon the properties of those deities—such as their appearance, enjoyments, and attendants—and the <term>kamma</term> <gloss>intentional action/deed</gloss> that generated them; or, because it is the cause of understanding the fruit of other actions. It is said, by whom was this spoken, where was it spoken, when was it spoken, and why was it spoken?

For this <term>Vimānavatthu</term> proceeds in two ways: by way of questions and by way of answers. In this, the answer-stanzas were spoken by the respective deities, but the question-stanzas were spoken partly by the Blessed One, partly by <term>Sakka</term> <gloss>the King of the gods</gloss> and others, and partly by the elder disciples. Among these, they were mostly spoken by the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, who is established in the position of the second chief disciple, who was placed by the Blessed One as the foremost among those possessing psychic power, who reached the summit of all the knowledge of the disciples' perfection—accompanied by the special qualities of the six higher knowledges and the four analytical knowledges—having accumulated the constituents of merit and knowledge for an <term>asaṃkheyya</term> <gloss>incalculable eon</gloss> and one hundred thousand <term>kappas</term> <gloss>aeons</gloss> for the status of the Blessed One's chief disciple, and having gradually fulfilled the perfections of a disciple. While speaking, he first spoke them while wandering in the realm of the gods for the benefit of the world by way of the deities' questions; then, after returning from there to the human world, he combined the questions and answers for the sake of making the fruit of merit manifest to humans.

<note>The original text contains footnotes referencing manuscript variations (S1, S2, B) and a specific citation to the Anguttara Nikāya (A. I, 23).</note>

## PROLEGOMENA

However, he himself expresses the true occasion shortly in the preface, because he saw many things being written by many, which were not sufficiently verified; and therefore he wanted to provide for posterity through his own work, so that the Church might have a verified and solid Evangelical history. And Eusebius (book 3, chapter 24), Epiphanius (book 2 against heresies), and Nicephorus acknowledge this occasion.

<margin>Argument: Luke started the history of the Gospel higher up than the others, etc.</margin>
He begins the Evangelical history higher up than the other two did, namely Matthew and Mark, who, with Luke, pursue the history of humanity above all. For not content to start the matter from the baptism of John and the genealogy of Christ, he also takes up those things that pertain to the conception of both Christ and John the Baptist: likewise the birth of both, and what happened in these times. From here he finally progresses to the doctrine of Christ; likewise, what he did. In miracles, he is diligent and copious; for he indicates the occasions, the fruits, and other circumstances. He adorns the life of Christ with human affections, and those ready to gratify, so that sin is absent: he everywhere assigns companions to Christ, disciples who are extremely simple, or crowds eager to learn: adversaries who are extremely persistent, the Jews, and from these, the Pharisees, the Chief Priests

For Socrates writes that it happened at the Council of Constantinople in the year 359 under the Emperor Constantius, *Ecclesiastical History* book II, 41; while Sozomen in *Ecclesiastical History* book VI, 37 (cf. the notes of Henri Valois), Theodoret in book IV, chapter 37, and Nicephorus Callistus in book IX, chapter 44, refer his defection to the times of Valens. Hence, who could doubt the faith of this version? Truly, those places which the Holy Fathers used against the Arians are all translated faithfully, and nothing appears in it from which it could be gathered that its author thought less correctly of Christ. Thomas Mareschallus, a most diligent observer of places that are awkwardly translated, confirms this with his testimony, and he speaks thus on page 483: *If I had observed anything in the Gothic texts that seemed to be argued as manifest Arianism (for I did not want to contend about uncertain suspicions), I would certainly not have hesitated to mark it with a black coal as the first.* And this is the reason why the same man conjectures (which Balthasar David Walther in *Officina Bibliothecae* § 300, page 246 for me, affirms without doubt) that Ulphilas completed this version before he transferred himself to the parts of the Arians, page 388, confer page 413. I also like to append what I found about this matter in Sixtus Senensis in *Bibliotheca* book IV, page 390: *Vulphilas first handed down to the Goths all the Divine Scriptures translated by himself from Greek into the Gothic language, and explained them in a Catholic manner, struggling long and much against the Arians.*

## V. It remains for me to add a few things concerning the Utility of the version.

This Version ought to be commended to us for two utilities primarily which it provides. Its use is significant (firstly) in explaining some controversial places and perplexed words, while it corroborates the true meaning with its consensus (aa). the length and width of the measure you hold, multiply them by themselves, and you will have the feet or the area of the measure whose sides you multiplied; by which, if you divide the feet of the surface to be divided, the quotient will show the sought amount. Thus, the <term>iugera</term> <gloss>acres</gloss> of the first mountain will be 18, and 1600 feet over. The <term>iugera</term> of the second mountain will be 24, and 88,000 feet over. The <term>iugera</term> of the third mountain will be 21, and 6400 feet. Let these things be said concerning the measurement of surfaces; now we must come to the dimension of bodies.

->Measurement of the thickness or solidity of a sphere.<-

The measurement of a body seeks the solidities and thicknesses of bodies, such as how many feet the magnitude of the body contains. So that you may attain some knowledge of this, I shall set forth the method of measuring or the <term>praxis</term> <gloss>practical application</gloss> of certain bodies, and first indeed, that of a sphere. Therefore, if you wish to investigate the solidity of a sphere, you should multiply its diameter cubically (that is, multiply it by itself once in a square, and multiply the product again by the diameter). This cube exceeds the thickness of the sphere. However, with the excess removed, the solidity of the sphere is left. Furthermore, the excess will be revealed by this way: Divide the cube by 12, and multiply the product by 10, and you will have the sought excess. Or, multiply the diameter cubically, and multiply the product by 11, and the 21st part of the whole sum gives the solidity of the sphere. Thus, the excess multiplied by 11 will also give the same. For example, let there be a sphere whose diameter is 7. The cube will be 343, the excess 163 and one third part, and the thickness of the sphere 179 and two thirds.

it can be much less of a wonder if the same should happen to the <term>unicornu</term>, which has indeed lacked a more accurate censure until now, besides that which was applied by the common people in their time, which, through longer progression, induces obscurity even in the most clear matters due to negligence. This eventually became all the greater because it is found very rarely and only in the treasuries of great princes. All of which could certainly have given the curious an opportunity to mix the true with the false, so that they might—if not substitute—at least admit into the place of the true <term>unicornu</term>, which they felt was held in delight by the magnates, fragments of perhaps burned horn, ivory, or other bones, or some kind of stones. In order for us to avoid such fraud, certain of the following signs seem entirely worthy of observation. But here, prudence and counsel are needed again, lest we seize upon and swear by false or superstitious things that are circulated as true and indubitable. Just as it is believed by the common people that the <term>unicornu</term> sweats in the presence of poison. Now, indeed, if it is asked whether and in what way it can happen that it emits a true sweat, the matter is quite stuck. To sweat is certainly an intrinsic effect excited by the benefit of the soul, and the <term>unicornu</term>, insofar as it is torn from the body and applied to medicine, lacks that soul; whence, therefore, the effect? Must one have recourse to occult qualities? But truly, neither do these act above their powers. Andreas Baccius, in the cited place, indeed reports that the horns of the <term>cerastes</term> <gloss>a species of snake</gloss> (a certain kind of snake, of which Albertus Magnus, Ulysses Aldrovandus, Lord Johannes Veslingius in Bartholinus, page 6, Jonston, and others make mention) as well as a certain kind of stone, of a glaucous, dark color, which they call "serpentine tongue," sweat in the presence of poison, but analogically or improperly; just as we see all polished and bright objects, surrounded by the humidity of the air, when heat approaches, altered in a certain way and as if emitting a sweat. But since that effect, or dimming, happens from elsewhere, even in the absence of poison, we are not to take it as some indubitable sign.

17. Superstitious, however, is that which Jordanus, Aldrovandus, and others report about the Venetian Jew and other charlatans who, by magical incantations, fascinated spiders, snakes, and scorpions so that they would not cross a defined circle, which they brought about by the benefit of rasped or ground <term>unicornu</term>. The blessed Sperling brought up the words in the German text in *Physical Institutions, book 6, chapter III, page 927*, from Basil's *Triumphwagen Antimonii*, page 66, which see. Where other modes of proof also exist simultaneously; for if a coin, excavated by art, is thrown into water so that it can swim freely here and there, then the <term>unicornu</term> is applied, though without corporal contact, the coin is immediately propelled by virtual contact in such a way that it seems to be taking flight. Conversely, put a piece of bread into a vessel filled with the purest water, and apply the <term>unicornu</term> in the way mentioned above, and you will see a wonderful effect, so that as you remove the <term>unicornu</term>, the bread also follows step by step, in the way that D. Kergerus, *On Ferments, sect. 1, c. 5, p. 46*, thinks, in which iron follows the magnet drawn by the same.

translation:

The first is called apparent, which is in the cognition of future things that can be known beforehand from these causes. Thus, a physician knows health or death beforehand. There is an order to such effects in knowing in some causes.

The second is prophecy improperly spoken, which communicates to someone prone to prophecy without such intelligence, according to what is held in Daniel 6: "There is need of intelligence in the vision." Jerome holds this same view in the beginning of his commentary on Isaiah. It happens that this occurs in three ways. In one way in a vision, thus Pharaoh saw ears of corn in a general way, and Belshazzar saw a hand writing on the wall (Daniel 7). The former was sleeping, the latter waking, yet neither of them was a prophet. But Daniel and Joseph, who understood the visions, were. Secondly, it happens in speech; thus Caiaphas (John 11) said a prophetic word, intending only to give counsel about the death of Christ, that it would be expedient, although he was innocent, lest the Romans come and take away their place and nation because of him. But this counsel was brought about by the Holy Spirit. He thus uttered that the death of Christ would be for the spiritual salvation of the whole world, while Caiaphas himself was ignorant of this; he was a rational animal, although through his tongue a rational word was uttered by an angel moving his tongue, without him knowing. Thirdly, this happens in operation, when the spirit moves someone to do something which has an outcome by itself, although the man moved is ignorant of the end; thus Judges 11 says of Jephthah that "the spirit of the Lord rushed upon him" to fight against the sons of Ammon, although future victory was not revealed to him. And such a motion is called the instinct of the Holy Spirit, which is a falling short of the definition of prophecy, according to the doctors, and such a motion is similar to the motion of the fortunate who moves toward something good without reason and prior knowledge, as is held in the book <term>On Good Fortune</term>. It differs, however, that the motion of the fortunate is from a natural cause, namely, from the influence of the heavens or the intelligence of the mover, as some say, or from both together, as others say. But the motion of Jephthah and Caiaphas is from a supernatural cause, namely, from the motion of the divine Spirit. This instinct approaches more closely to the definition of prophecy than the other two modes proposed. The third is prophecy true and properly spoken, which is understood as prophecy that is also found in a multiple degree, of which one is more excellent than the other; hence, for the rest, there is clearer intelligence. The first degree of this prophecy is that which, when communicated with a vision, is given with the intelligence of the vision; thus Jeremiah sees a burning pot and its face from the face of the north (Jeremiah 1), and he understood and this was signified as the army of the king of Babylon about to come to burn the city of Jerusalem.
The second degree, which is not such a vision or appearance, but hearing a voice instructing about something supernatural. 1 Kings 3: Samuel heard the voice of the Lord speaking, and yet he did not see any figure appearing to him.

There are three things he treats in the whole epistle. In the beginning, he corrects in the <term>Corinthians</term> those vices which seemed light to them and not at all worthy of notice: therefore, they had not sought the Apostle's judgment on these. Because these were the gravest, he proposes them in the first place, such as were the dissensions and sects on account of teachers; the vain persuasion by which they sought eloquence in the ministers of the Lord; fornication; incest; and the habit of litigating before infidel judges. They cared little for these and similar things. These are treated up to the seventh chapter. In the second part, he responds to the questions of the <term>Corinthians</term>, which in good part were born from the contention of the teachers and had rendered the listeners ambiguous. Such are the questions moved concerning marriage in chapter 7; concerning the choice of foods, namely concerning things sacrificed to idols; concerning idols; and in chapter 11, concerning ecclesiastical assemblies and the avoiding of women. Also, lest they teach publicly, or rather, lest they have any right of questioning; concerning the <term>Supper of the Lord</term>; concerning the use of spiritual gifts; concerning the excellence of the prophetic office; concerning the <term>resurrection of the dead</term>, and the like up to chapter 16. translation:
we believe that youth should be instructed in those things whose use is in old age. These things are indeed small, as most people think; but, says Livy, by not despising those small things, our ancestors made this state great. See how wisely the Paduan Siren attributes the magnitude of empire to the education of youth! And certainly, citizens will be such as the young are. Therefore, encourage your own with your presence, especially since an examination both calls and invites you. And, as my Symmachus says, piety even wants you to become young again, so that shared labor may instill the sweetness of literature in your children. Indeed, it is ingrained in good minds that they themselves should generously bestow upon all what they abundantly desire from others. This is what we wish, what we desire and expect. Therefore, given on September 3, 1635.

In the name of the Lord, we begin to write a commentary on Tractate Berakhot.

Rabbi Judah said in the name of Rav: What is the meaning of that which is written, "When you take the sum of the children of Israel according to their number, then they shall give every man a ransom for his soul to the Lord, when you number them; that there be no plague among them, when you number them" <note>Exodus 30:12</note>. 
It is taught: Rabbi Judah says, three commandments were the Israelites commanded upon their entry into the land: to appoint a king for themselves, to cut off the seed of Amalek, and to build for themselves the Chosen House <note>The Holy Temple</note>.
Rabbi Nehorai says: This passage was only said regarding the future, that they would stand in them <note>i.e., fulfill them later</note>.
And so it says, "When you take the sum of the children of Israel according to their number."
How is it understood that this "numbering" <term>pekudah</term> <gloss>numbering/command</gloss> is a term of importance? 
It is written here "when you number them" <term>bifkod etam</term>, and it is written there "when you number them."
Just as there it is an importance, so too here it is an importance.
Rav Ashi said: Learn from this that one who wishes to count the Israelites should not count them by the head <note>i.e., by individual tally, which is demeaning</note>.
For it is written, "that there be no plague among them when you number them."
Rav Isaac said: Anyone who counts Israel transgresses a negative commandment, as it is stated, "Yet the number of the children of Israel shall be as the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured nor counted" <note>Hosea 2:1</note>.
Rav Nachman bar Isaac said: There are those who say "neither measured nor counted."
It is taught: Rabbi Isaac says, what is the meaning of that which is written, "And he shall give the silver as a ransom for his soul"?
This teaches that each and every one gives half a shekel.
What is the reason? Rav Assi said: In order that they might atone for the deed of the Calf, as it is written, "And he shall give the silver as a ransom for his soul to the Lord when you number them."
Rav Judah said in the name of Rav: What is the meaning of that which is written, "And you shall be to Me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation"? 
"These are the words which you shall speak to the children of Israel."
Rav Hanina bar Papa said: What is the meaning of that which is written, "And Moses took the tent and pitched it outside the camp"?
This teaches that Moses, our teacher—peace be upon him—would separate himself from the public so that he would be free to engage in Torah and wisdom.
Rav Judah said in the name of Rav: Whoever engages in Torah for its own sake, the Torah becomes for him a potion of life, as it is stated, "It is a tree of life to those who take hold of it."
And whoever engages in Torah not for its own sake, the Torah becomes for him a potion of death, as it is stated, "My doctrine shall drop as the rain."
Rav said: May the Merciful One save us from such a concept.
Rav Judah said in the name of Rav: What is the meaning of that which is written, "And the Lord spoke unto Moses face to face, as a man speaks unto his friend"?
This teaches that the Holy One, blessed be He, spoke with Moses gently, in the way that a person speaks with his friend.
Rav Chisda said: What is the meaning of that which is written, "And he would return to the camp, but his servant Joshua the son of Nun, a young man, would not depart from the tent"?
This teaches that Joshua would serve Moses in all his needs and would not move from the House of Study.
Rav Judah said in the name of Rav: Happy is he who merits to serve the Sages, for through this he merits to learn Torah and fear of Heaven.
Blessed be He who gives strength to the weary and increases power to the powerless.

### Uiber die Entstehung der Feuer speyenden Berge.

---

Die Vulkane entstehen stets auf folgende Art: Es öffnet sich an einem niedrigen Orte im flachen Erdreiche ein Feuerschlund. Die Oeffnung desselben wirft eine Menge brennender Stoffe aus, welche zum Theil als Lava herabfließen, zum Theil in die Luft empor steigen und in Gestalt eines Hagels herabfallen. Diese Materien bilden einen Kegel, gerade so, wie durch aufgeworfene Erde der Maulwurfs-Hügel, oder durch den herabfallenden Sand der kleine Hügel im untern Theile einer Sand-Uhr entsteht. Der Canal, durch welchen diese Materien gehen, bleibt in der Mitte dieses Kegels allezeit offen, so lange die Ausbrüche dauern. Wenn neue Oeffnungen auf einem Berge entstehen, so sind es wahrscheinlich alte und bloß aufs neue geöffnete Feuerschlünde: ein ganz neues Feuer bricht allezeit da, wo die Rinde am dünnsten ist, d. i. in den Planen und Thälern, nicht in den Bergen aus, wenn sich nicht daselbst schon alte vorher geöffnete Canale befinden. ### On the Origin of Fire-Spitting Mountains.

---

Volcanoes always originate in the following manner: a fire-throat opens at a low spot in flat terrain. The opening throws out a quantity of burning materials, which partly flow down as lava and partly ascend into the air, falling down in the form of hail. These materials form a cone, just as a molehill is formed by thrown-up earth, or a small mound is formed at the bottom of an hourglass by falling sand. The channel through which these materials pass always remains open in the center of this cone as long as the eruptions continue. If new openings form on a mountain, they are likely old fire-throats that have merely been reopened: a completely new fire always breaks out where the crust is thinnest, i. e., in the plains and valleys, not in the mountains, unless there are already old, previously opened channels there. However, the fire-spitting mountains themselves, whose materials lie one upon the other without order or firm connection, are very easily penetrated by fire. ## ABSOLUTION

<margin>11.</margin>It is asked: Which of the words of absolution: *I absolve you from your sins in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit*, belong to the essence of the form, and are necessary for the validity of the sacrament?

Answer: Although the learned doctors <note>theologians</note> disagree among themselves, and others have written that these words, *from your sins*, are only of the necessity of a precept and do not pertain to the essence of the form, and teach that these words are sufficient: *I absolve you*; nevertheless, it cannot be denied that there is greater probability in the opinion stating that those words, *from your sins*, also pertain to the essence of the form. For that is the opinion of the majority, and it seems to be gathered from the Council of Trent, session 14, chapter 3. Especially because those words, *I absolve you*, are indifferent to absolution from *sins and censures*. Therefore, so that they may signify specifically absolution from *sins*, they must be determined by these: *from your sins*. Since, therefore, that opinion is safer, undoubtedly he who omits them exposes the Sacrament to the danger of nullity, because when dealing with the validity of the sacraments, the safer path must always be followed according to the decree of Innocent XII condemning proposition 1.

First, he establishes a <term>prodiēgēma</term> <gloss>preface/preliminary narration</gloss>, which is again accommodated for benevolence. *I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers*, i.e., of our affliction, which happened to us in Asia. He commends himself by the name of brother, because he acknowledges them as brothers. Next, because he admonishes them fraternally in a useful matter. *I do not want you to be ignorant*. They seemed destined to remain ignorant, unless the Apostle opened the true causes. For the malevolent were intentionally hiding the truth here, but the good were fewer, and the better could not be heard; therefore, the truth had to be confirmed, nay, explained, by the Apostle. Then he establishes the proposition of the narration. For he is about to narrate his Asian affliction. This is the place of docility. For he shows what matter he is going to act upon here. He had indeed suffered other infinite persecutions, but they did not pertain to the present matter. Furthermore, what that affliction was is not sufficiently certain. There are those who think it is the one in Acts 19, which was excited at Ephesus by Demetrius, but it is possible that it was some other much greater one, which was not written down by Luke.

II The narration itself concerning the magnitude of the affliction connects the parts through <term>aitiologian</term> <gloss>a causal account</gloss> (<term>hoti kath' hyperbolēn</term> <gloss>because beyond measure</gloss>). The magnitude makes for an excuse, which consists of three members. First, *I was burdened beyond strength*. There is a metaphor in the word <term>ebarēthēmen</term> <gloss>we were burdened</gloss>. For those are said to be burdened upon whom a greater weight is imposed, as if you were to impose a burden upon a boy that was meant for robust men. From this, therefore, he takes his excuse: The affliction was unequal to my strength, therefore I should not be accused.

Besides the present work, which was printed in Paris in the year 1718, he brought to light many others that acquired him supreme reputation, and he left many others still unpublished upon dying. The Relations that we report here are drawn from a manuscript of the Library of the Count of Seignelay, and are the work of two Arab merchants, the first of whom traveled to China in the year 237 of the Hijra, that is to say, the year 861 of Christ; the other in 264 of the aforementioned Hijra, that is, 877 of the Christian Era. The first of these Relations is missing its beginning, and is also mutilated in the middle: the other is whole, and bears the name of the Arab Author, who is Abuzeid el Hasen of Siraf. They deserve much esteem, both for their antiquity, and for the simplicity with which they are written, and for the abundance of rare news that they contain within themselves. Everyone knows that the first Writer who treated of China with some foundation was Marco Polo the Venetian, who returned from his Travels in the East in the year 1295, whence the relation of these two Arabs boasts 400 years of antiquity over him. They are eyewitnesses, and in such a manner, without trickery or affectation, they narrate the things seen by them that they command complete faith. There are so many particularities that they describe, both regarding the quality of the country and concerning the customs of the Chinese, that delight results equal to the utility. See how the drink of Tea is described to us: "They call it Sah, and it is a small shrub that gives more leaves than the pomegranate tree, and whose odor is more pleasant, but which tastes a bit bitter. Water is boiled and poured over the leaf; and this drink makes them recover from every ailment." 6. Nec verò ad Theologiam referenda est Pnevmatologia. Quia (1) hæ duæ disciplinæ diversis nituntur principijs. Illa quippe principia sua non nisi ex revelatione habet. Hæc verò sua principia ex naturâ habet congenita, partim etiam per sensum, experientiam et inductionem acquirit. Quia (2) Pnevmatologia est una ex disciplinis Theoreticis ipsa verò Theologia est practica vel Theoretico-Practica seu mixta. Quia (3) Pnevmatica nec dignitate omnes doctrinas antecellit nec ordine Doctrinæ est ultima, At Theologia est omnium eminentissima et ultima si doctrinam spectes, utpote quæ à Deo singulari consilio emanavit, iterumque nos ad Deum ducendo unde venerat tendit. Ergò Pnevmatica ad Theologiam pertinere non potest. Vide Paulus Voëtius in Theologiâ Naturali Reformatâ capitulo 1. numero 5. pagina 7.

7. Manet itaque Conclusio nostra Vera quod videlicet peculiaris aliqua disciplina Spiritibus in Philosophiâ assignanda sit à reliquis omnibus distincta. Probatum id jam est per remotionem ab illis disciplinis ad quas referri posse videbatur, et porrò probatur argumento gemino: (1) Positâ objecti formalis diversitate diversa ponitur disciplina. Atqui in doctrinâ Spirituum ponitur objecti formalis diversitas. Ergò etiam ponitur diversa disciplina. (2) Si Spiritus in nullâ disciplinâ se habet vel ut principium vel ut affectio, vel ut modus contrahens, ad nullam etiam debet referri. Atqui verum est prius. Ergò et posterius.

8. Redarguuntur hîc ij, qui integra universæ Philosophiæ volumina edentes nullam tamen mentionem doctrinæ

But these are given in the doctrine of Spirits and in the doctrine of natural body. Therefore, two distinct disciplines are given. We supersede the proof of the premises for this time, since they can be manifest to anyone, and there is no long controversy in this matter.

6. Nor, indeed, should Pneumatology be referred to Theology. Because (1) these two disciplines rely on diverse principles. For the latter has its principles solely from revelation. But the former has its principles innate from nature, and in part also acquires them through sense, experience, and induction. Because (2) Pneumatology is one of the Theoretical disciplines, whereas Theology itself is practical, or Theoretical-Practical, or mixed. Because (3) Pneumatics neither surpasses all doctrines in dignity nor is it the final doctrine in order; but Theology is the most eminent and final of all if you look at the doctrine, inasmuch as it emanated from God by singular counsel and, by leading us back to God, tends toward where it had come. Therefore, Pneumatics cannot belong to Theology. See Paulus Voëtius in <term>Theologia Naturalis Reformata</term> <gloss>Reformed Natural Theology</gloss>, Chapter 1, number 5, page 7.

7. Thus, our Conclusion remains True: that, namely, some peculiar discipline is to be assigned to Spirits in Philosophy, distinct from all others. This has already been proven by removal from those disciplines to which it seemed it could be referred, and it is further proven by a double argument: (1) Given the diversity of the formal object, a diverse discipline is posited. But in the doctrine of Spirits, the diversity of the formal object is posited. Therefore, a diverse discipline is also posited. (2) If Spirit in no discipline acts either as a principle, or as an affection, or as a contracting mode, it should not be referred to any. But the former is true. Therefore, the latter is also.

These are the words of Strabo: In Crete, Jove's rites are also performed with orgies. They called Curetes certain youths who would dance in armor. And they add a fable about the BIRTHDAYS OF JUPITER, that Saturn was accustomed to swallow his children as soon as they were born. Rhea, however, tried to hide the pains of childbirth secretly and to lead the infant away when brought forth, and to save him as much as possible: for to this, the assistance of the Curetes who, armed with drums and other clattering instruments, would dance, terrifying Saturn with the tumult around the Goddess, and deceiving him while stealing away the son: by the same labor it is handed down that the Jove nurtured by them was fed. They think Curetes were called quasi-curators, either because they performed the <term>κουροτροφίαν</term> <gloss>nurturing of the boy</gloss> of Jove, or because they ministered to him. Which Suidas explains when he asserts that the Curetes were the nurses and guardians of Jove.

Arnobius, *Against the Gentiles*, book 3, commemorates those Curetes who are said to have hidden Jove's wailing with cymbals at one time, at another the fingers of Samothrace, which the Greeks indicate are five, and are called Idaean Dactyls. And elsewhere: *Was Jove not saved from destruction by the kindness of the Curetes?* Whom they then led away to the hidden places of Mount Ida: Thence Crete is called the island of the great Jove. The commentary of Servius, in book 4 of the Georgics, page 149, contributes to our matter: Ops, the wife of Saturn, gave Jove to the Curetes, Corybantes, and Idaean Dactyls to be guarded, on Mount Dictae in Crete, lest Saturn consume him, as he was accustomed to do with all his sons.

The robed Mistress of frauds, the Augusta consort of the royal couch, steps into the arena: the supreme Commander of wars, Porphyrius, steps forth, accompanied by two cohorts of soldiers: the Augustus Emperor of the East, Maximinus, steps forth, offering the tender Virgin eloquence and majesty, the honeyed lures of pleasures, blandishments, and enticements, more powerful for persuading than all torments. What of these things, CATHARINE? With a brief but sharp diction, she stripped Augusta, the wife of Maximinus, and Porphyrius, the invincible Commander of the royal Army, of the arms of Impiety, clothed them with the breastplate of justice and the helmet of salvation, and captivated them in obedience to faith. The phoenix of geniuses, Virgil, tells of the oleaster tree of Hercules, dried up by the unfairness of time, fruitful of no leaves, endowed with no greenery, having sprouted again when joined to the Laurel with cut trunks, spread into branches, curled into leaves, and provided opaque shade for travelers. So much it profited to be joined to the Laurel. Let us elicit the kernel of truth from the bark of fables, audience. Augusta, the Wife of Maximinus, who had withered in the barren sand of gentility, joined to the crowned Laurel CATHARINE, put on the greenery of the orthodox faith, curls into leaves, spreads into branches, abounds in the fruit of Christian fortitude, crowned against the lightning of Maximinus by the victorious Laurel, the glory of Tiberius Caesar who bore the Laurel in a troubled sky, takes heroic fortitude from the lightning of threats, courage from scourges, goads from the wheel, strength from swords; she blunts the rushing North winds of the lead-weighted ones with the boss of her branches, and with shading and dripping branches pours the juice of the true faith into dead stumps, animates them into life, and clothes them in greenery and the adornment of glory. But as the fire of fury rekindles in the heart of Maximinus from Stygian fires, the savage Tyranny burdens the Laurel with Chains: Do you not know that the tall tree of Xerxes is honored, not burdened, by the knots bound through chains? The burning rabies of the Tyrant puts coals under the Laurel: Do you not know that the Laurel shines more illustriously from the rays of more flames? Do you not know that the Laurel of the Ammonian grove, subjected to the most burning fires of the Pole, abounds in the greenery of leaves? Do you not know that the Byzantine olive, sprinkled with a fiery rain, budding with new leaves, explains its top more highly? Strip the Laurel, peel off the bark, cut the neck: The milk-white neck will emanate snow-white rivulets of milk, and will drip purple from the barbed fountains of the veins, so that it may quench the burning thirst of the Tyrant with Blood; And may the lilies of Virgin candor, akin to the purple roses of the Martyrs, clearly manifest the Victorious Laurel CATHARINE, akin to the crowned Laurel. The Tyrant orders the crowned Laurel to be struck down by the sword of the lictor. The crowned laurel falls, prostrate in body, erect in countenance, sublime in mind, higher than the earth it falls to the earth, so that it may press with its body, trample with its feet, elude with its breast, whatever savors of the vanity of a fleeting world. <margin></margin>
What were you?
Putrid sperm.

**W**hy do you swell with pride, man? Why are you vainly arrogant?
Behold the humble beginnings of your life.
Once you were fluid sperm, a tiny bubble
Distended by breath, enclosed in a very small space.
In a small and vile place, or dark prison,
Urine was a wall for you, filth was a wall for you.

Persian treasure does not tame your golden thirst.

<margin></margin>
What are you?
A vessel of excrement.

While you mix heaven and earth with tumult,
What are you meanwhile, if not a vessel of excrement?

Food for worms.

Rotten food for worms, earth, ash, nothing.

Who formed you, the heavens, the lands, the seas, all things with a word,

fred. ad Rubricam Codex de Advocatis lex 1. littera g.
Quare autem Advocati dicantur **Togati** & **Scholastici** id si quis scire desideret adeat *Rittershusius* qui ad *Novellas* pagina 9. capitulo 8. numero 8. & sequuntur ex *Casaubono* ad *Capitolinum* posterius elegantius declarat ostendendo indici Scholasticos quia in Scholis fictis litibus & declamationibus quas *meletas* & meditationes appellabant se exercere soliti sunt. Advocare autem quod sicut diximus, officium hic denotat sumitur saepissime active ut in lex 18. *Digesta Rem ratam haberi* vide *Bachovius* ad τὰ πρῶτα titulus de Postulatione numero 1. pagina mea 742.

§. 10. Et sunt hi nihil aliud quam personae publicae quae litigantibus in judicio adsistunt consilio causam adjuvando vel legitime & recte proponendo deducendoque vide lex 6. §. 1. Codex de Postulatione lex 11. §. 1. Codex de Advocatis lege *Bachovius* ad τὰ πρῶτα titulus de Postulatione numero 1. *Seneca de brevitate vitae* capitulo 2. Dominus *Georgius Adam Struvius Exercitatio* 7. ad *Digesta* pagina 1. thesi 3. ex quo apparet qui alias dicuntur **Auscultantes**, ut in **Flandria** passim, proprie non esse Advocatos. Utpote cum illi nullas partium causas defendant, neutri partium serviant, nihil in judiciis orent, sed propterea saltem assumantur ut post adeptam juris scientiam stylum judicii addiscant, & procedendi modum observent, vide *Damhouderius Praxis rerum Civilium* capitulo 96. numero 2.

<column-break/>

§. 11. **Dicimus in Iudicio.** Et recte: non modo si judiciorum ordinem solemnem ante sublatas per Constantinum Imperatorem formulas respiciamus, sed & imprimis si rem secundum Dicasteria nostra examinemus. Iure enim Civili quamvis Postulatio seu Advocatio videatur pertinere ad jus, seu, ut apertius loquamur, ad ea judicia quae coram Magistratu superiori instituuntur argumentum lex 4. §. 8. *Digesta de damno infecto* verbi gratia Praetore vide lex 1. principium *Digesta de Postulatione* liquet tamen alios textus conjungentibus non minus recte quoque apud Magistratum inferiorem postulari vide Dominus *Henricus Hahnius* ad *Wesenbecium* titulus de Postulatione numero 2. pagina mea 439. quod & contra eundem vel per Senatusconsultum vel per Interpretationem prudentum ad judicem quoque Pedaneum pertinuisse arbitramur, propter lex 1. §. 6. versu item Senatusconsulto *Digesta de Postulatione* vide *Bachovius* ad τὰ πρῶτα titulus de Postulatione numero 1. pagina mea 743. *Gaddius de Verborum Significatione* ad lex 10. numero 2. & sequuntur *Brissonius* libro 5. *formularum populi Romani* quem adducit *Treutlerus* volumine 1. disputatio 8. thesi 1. littera B. **Hodiè Pedaneos Iudices** hoc est ad certam formulam adstrictos & nihil ultra nisi simplicem rei notionem sibi vindicantes non habemus vide lex 1. 2. Codex de Pedaneis judicibus *Paulus Christinaeus* volumine 2. decisionum 151. numero 1. 2. & sequitur *Groenewegen* ad titulus Codex qui pro sua iurisdictione iudices dare numero 1. & 2. sed propria omnibus competit Iurisdictio
