<vocab>Advocati, Scholastici, Togati, meletas, Digesta, Codex, Novellas, Postulatio, Auscultantes, Dicasteria, Pedaneos Iudices, Iurisdictio, Rittershusius, Bachovius, Struvius, Damhouderius, Hahnius, Wesenbecium, Brissonius, Treutlerus, Christinaeus, Groenewegen</vocab>
translation:
to the rubric of the Code <note>original: "Codex"</note> on Advocates, law 1, letter g.
If anyone desires to know why advocates are called **Togati** <gloss>wearing the toga</gloss> and **Scholastici** <gloss>scholastics</gloss>, let him approach *Rittershusius*, who, at page 9, chapter 8, number 8 and following of his commentary on the *Novellae* <gloss>New Constitutions</gloss>, declares it more elegantly from *Casaubon* on the *Capitolinus* <note>referring to an author of the Historia Augusta</note>, showing they are called scholastics because they were accustomed to exercise themselves in the schools with mock disputes and declamations, which they called *meletas* <gloss>exercises/practice pieces</gloss> and meditations. Moreover, "to advocate" <term>advocare</term>, which as we said denotes the office here, is most often taken actively, as in law 18, *Digest* on "ratification of acts." See *Bachovius* on the *ta prota* <gloss>first things</gloss>, title on Postulation, number 1, page 742 of my copy.

§. 10. And these are nothing other than public persons who assist those litigating in court by helping the cause with counsel or by legally and correctly proposing and presenting it. See law 6, §. 1, Code on Postulation; law 11, §. 1, Code on Advocates; read *Bachovius* on *ta prota*, title on Postulation, number 1; *Seneca, On the Brevity of Life*, chapter 2; Lord *Georgius Adam Struvius*, Exercise 7 on the *Digest*, page 1, thesis 3. From this it appears that those who are otherwise called **Auscultantes** <gloss>listeners/auditors</gloss>, as in **Flanders** in many places, are not properly advocates. For they defend none of the parties' causes, serve neither party, and plead nothing in court; they are assumed only so that, after obtaining a knowledge of law, they may learn the style of the court and observe the manner of proceeding. See *Damhouderius, Practice of Civil Matters*, chapter 96, number 2.

<column-break/>

§. 11. **We say: in Court.** And correctly so: not only if we look at the solemn order of courts before the formulas were abolished by the Emperor Constantine, but also especially if we examine the matter according to our own courts <term>Dicasteria</term> <gloss>tribunals/courts</gloss>. For by Civil Law, although postulation or advocacy seems to pertain to the law—or, to speak more openly, to those trials that are instituted before a superior magistrate (argument from law 4, §. 8, *Digest* on "damage not yet done," for example, the Praetor; see law 1, the beginning of *Digest* on Postulation)—it is nevertheless clear from combining other texts that it is no less correctly petitioned before an inferior magistrate. See Lord *Henricus Hahnius* on *Wesenbecius*, title on Postulation, number 2, page 439 of my copy. We also judge that this pertains to the <term>pedaneous</term> <gloss>inferior/lower</gloss> judge, either by <term>Senatusconsultum</term> <gloss>decree of the senate</gloss> or by the interpretation of the learned, because of law 1, §. 6, at the verse "likewise by Senate decree," *Digest* on Postulation. See *Bachovius* on *ta prota*, title on Postulation, number 1, page 743 of my copy; *Gaddius, On the Signification of Words*, on law 10, number 2 and following; *Brissonius*, book 5 of *The Formulas of the Roman People*, whom *Treutlerus* cites in volume 1, disputation 8, thesis 1, letter B. **Today we do not have Pedaneous Judges** <gloss>inferior judges tied to a formula</gloss>, that is, judges restricted to a certain formula and claiming nothing for themselves beyond a simple notion of the matter. See law 1, 2, Code on Pedaneous Judges; *Paulus Christinaeus*, volume 2, decision 151, numbers 1 and 2; and *Groenewegen* on the title of the Code "Which judges for their own jurisdiction," numbers 1 and 2. But jurisdiction itself belongs to all.

§. 23. Finally, when the barbarous race of the Saracens occupied the Holy Land, they devastated most things, erased the traces of Christian life, and changed almost the very face of the Holy Land; there can be no doubt that they also brought violence against the cave of Christ's nativity and seized the gold and other most precious ornaments with their own rapacious hands, so that many things which are shown there today are, if not counterfeit, at least uncertain. These things would have to be explained at greater length if they did not seem to exceed our allotted space. We therefore leave this stony cave of Christ's nativity, and we take our newborn <term>JESULUM</term> <gloss>little Jesus</gloss> with us from it, and, bound in the swaddling clothes of pure faith, we place him in the humble cave of our heart—thoroughly renewed and carved from the rock by the firmness of good purpose—adorning it not with gold or marble, but seasoning it with the myrrh of serious repentance, which is mildly bitter and of most sweet odor before God.

<header>LIBER PRIMVS.</header>

but the union of the body with the concord of members under one spirit, the form of the society: but the intention of living well has the proximate final cause: but the desire for attaining the future has the final intention, for which other things are constituted. And from all these is gathered the necessity of administration, which may conform to the intention, and lead it to effect, and preserve it; and it is taught that a principality, just like a single spirit, and the art of ruling, is required no less than in a physical body, that of one man. Reason in the soul and the intellect of things to be done, and those which must be commanded to be executed by individual members. The members of one man are not suitable for all actions, but must be preserved and informed under their own. The foot cannot see, the eye cannot walk, the ear cannot touch, the hand cannot hear, because it does not have the instrument or organ for that. Nor does the soul, which knows the faculty and action of each member, command the same things, but its own proper things, and thus it cares entirely for each with its own proper care, an example of which the prudent administration that presides over the body of society follows, and foresees and provides for what is convenient for each member or man. First and especially it regards the whole body of the people, then also individuals: lest while it only considers the whole, with the parts despised, from which the whole is perfected, the whole itself may fail.

It is furthermore evident that a mixed body is not composed of only four elements. Finally, it is clear that it is a vain labor to deduce all physical mutations and generations from a varied temperament of them and their qualities. Therefore, let these dusty and trivial wars depart, which Galen, Aristotle, Avicenna, Averroës, and others have brought into the kingdom of natural philosophy. XXXIV. Postremò Duratio alia est creata, alia increata. Increata est propria solius DEI, diciturque Æternitas; et definitur à Boëtio: *Intermi- nabilis vitæ tota simul et perfecta possessio.* Duratio creata alia est temporaria, a- lia perpetua. ### DE QVANTITATE.

XXXV. Quantum describit Aristoteles hîc lib. 5. tex 18. *Quod est divisibile in ea, quæ insunt, quorum utrumque vel unumquodque unum quid, et hoc aliquid aptum est esse.* Id est (ut quidem P. Suarez interpretatur) quorum v- trumque aptum est naturâ suâ per sese, ut unum quoddam totum, ab alijs separatum, manere, et quidem quantum est ex vi quantitatis, eodem modo di- visibile, divisibilitate scilicet Physicâ, et naturali, vi cuius unum Corpus naturaliter expellit aliud, vel partes eius à loco, quem ante occupabant.

XXXVI. Est sententia, ut ait P. Suarez, inter Thomistas satis vul- garis, primarium quantitatis effectum formalem esse distinctionem par- tium integralium; ita ut sine quantitate nec Materia prima, nec ulla alia entitas materialis aliquas partes integrantes habeat. Thomistas ex Nostris secutus est P. Vasquez tom. 3. in 3. p. d. 190. à n. 20. Sed contrà 1. Nam sicuti vnaquæque res per se ipsam est ens, ita per se ipsam est vna, et conse- quenter divisa et distincta à quovis alio. 2. Quia aliàs procedendum foret in infinitum. Nam si vna res est distincta ab aliâ per aliam entitatem tertiam, ergo ab illâ tertiâ debebit iterum distingui per aliam quartam, et sic in infini- tum. 3. Quia Materia supponitur ad quantitatem cum totâ suâ entitate. Ergo non potest accipere partes ab illâ: cùm enim totum nihil aliud sit, quàm omnes partes, quod supponitur cum totâ entitate, debet etiam supponi cum partibus. Non potest ergo primarius effectus formalis quantitatis consistere in distinctio- ne partium.

XXXIII. Regarding Imaginary Time we judge the same as we do regarding Imaginary space, namely that it is in reality nothing, beyond the intrinsic durations of things which found various relations of distance and nearness.

XXXIV. Finally, duration is either created or uncreated. The uncreated is proper to GOD alone, and is called Eternity; and it is defined by <term>Boethius</term> <gloss>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius, Roman philosopher</gloss>: *The whole, simultaneous, and perfect possession of interminable life.* Created duration is either temporary or perpetual. It is temporary if it has both a beginning and an end. It is perpetual if it at least has no end. Such is the duration of Angels and the rational soul, which is also called <term>Aevum</term> <gloss>the Age or Eon</gloss>, and is commonly defined as: *The uninterrupted permanence of a thing in being once received.*

### ON QUANTITY.

XXXV. <term>Aristotle</term> describes a quantity here in Book 5, text 18: *That which is divisible into those things which are present, of which each one or every one is a certain "one," and this "something" is apt to be.* That is (as Father <term>Suarez</term> indeed interprets) of which each one is apt by its own nature in and of itself, as a certain whole, separated from others, to remain, and indeed, insofar as it is from the force of quantity, divisible in the same way, namely by physical and natural divisibility, by the force of which one Body naturally expels another, or its parts from the place which they previously occupied.

XXXVI. It is an opinion, as Father <term>Suarez</term> says, sufficiently common among the <term>Thomists</term> <gloss>followers of Thomas Aquinas</gloss>, that the primary formal effect of quantity is the distinction of integral parts; so that without quantity neither primary matter nor any other material entity has any integral parts. Father <term>Vasquez</term> <gloss>Gabriel Vázquez, Jesuit theologian</gloss> followed the Thomists among our own in Volume 3, part 3, disputation 190, from number 20. But to the contrary: 1. For just as each thing is a being in and of itself, so it is "one" in and of itself, and consequently divided and distinct from anything else. 2. Because otherwise one would have to proceed to infinity. For if one thing is distinct from another by another third entity, then it must be distinguished from that third by another fourth, and so on to infinity. 3. Because matter is presupposed for quantity with its whole entity. Therefore, it cannot receive parts from it; for since the whole is nothing other than all its parts, that which is presupposed with its whole entity must also be presupposed with its parts. Therefore, the primary formal effect of quantity cannot consist in the distinction of parts.

### Oleum Cicinum.

GELISCO, nouae Hispaniae prouincia, oleum seu liquor quidam adfertur, cui, oleum ficus infernalis, Hispani nomen indiderunt, eo quod ex arbore cum fructu, tum foliis simili Ricino, sed in maiorem altitudinem, ob soli ubertatem, excrescente, elicitur.

<margin>Oleum ficus infernalis.</margin>

Eadem uero ratione hoc oleum Indi eliciunt, quam docuit Dioscorides lib. 1. cap. 30. hoc est, contuso semine, deinde in aqua cocto, postremum oleo innatante cochlearibus excepto. Hec eliciendorum oleorum ratio e feminibus & fructibus, Indis admodum familiaris est, quippe qui nullam expressionem norint: sed etiam hoc oleum isto modo quam expressione facilius elicitur.

<margin>Oleorum eliciendorum ratio.</margin>

Magnis uiribus pollet istud oleum, ueluti experientia, & multo eius usu comprobatum est, cum in India, tum in his regionibus. Omnes morbos ab humoribus frigidis prouenientes sanat, omnes tumores dissoluit, flatusque discutit, praesertim uentris, eamque ob causam non modo in Anasarca utile, sed in omnibus hydropisis generibus, si, uentre illo inuncto, aliquot guttae uino aut alio liquore commodo excepte forbeatur, etenim aquas euacuat, quod etiam minore noxa facit, clysteribus iniectum. Ventriculum frigidis humoribus & flatibus liberat: & coli doloribus utile, si partes affectae eo inungantur, & aliquot guttulae sumantur. Efficacius subuenit

translation:
<header>CARAÑA.</header>

It dissolves inveterate tumors and stops defluxions of cold or mixed humors: it is very useful for any pains of the nerves and brain: and it heals recent wounds, especially of the nerves and joints, without any other added medicine. It represses defluxions into the eyes and other parts when applied behind the ears and to the temples. It exceeds the second degree of heat. It is collected, like the former, by wounding trees.

But from the same Cartagena, a province of the new kingdom, a certain Caraña, purer and as clear as crystal, was brought to us, much more excellent, useful, and fragrant than the former.

### Oleum Cicinum.

From JELISCO, a province of New Spain, a certain oil or liquor is brought, to which the Spaniards have given the name "oil of the hellish fig," for the reason that it is extracted from a tree similar in both fruit and leaves to the castor bean <term>Ricinus</term>, but growing to a greater height on account of the richness of the soil.

<margin>Oil of the hellish fig.</margin>

The Indians extract this oil in the same manner that Dioscorides taught in book 1, chapter 30: that is, by crushing the seed, then boiling it in water, and finally skimming off the oil that floats on top with spoons. This method of extracting oils from seeds and fruits is very familiar to the Indians, who know of no pressing: but this oil is also extracted more easily in this way than by pressing.

<margin>Method of extracting oils.</margin>

This oil possesses great powers, as has been proven by experience and its much use, both in India and in these regions. It heals all diseases arising from cold humors, dissolves all tumors, and dispels flatulence, especially of the belly; and for this reason, it is useful not only in <term>anasarca</term> <gloss>dropsy of the flesh</gloss> but in all kinds of <term>hydropisis</term> <gloss>dropsy</gloss> if, after the belly is anointed with it, a few drops are taken in wine or another suitable liquid, for it evacuates waters, which it also does with less harm when injected as a <term>clyster</term> <gloss>enema</gloss>. that some of the Jews fasted twice in every week, namely on the second and fifth days, is evident not only from the example of that Pharisee whose mention is made in Luke, but is also clearly implied in the Babylonian Talmud, Tractate *Bava Kama* <note>(u)</note>. The teachers of the Hebrews in the Jerusalem Talmud, Tractate *Megillah* <note>(x)</note>, give this reason for this matter: that Moses ascended the mountain on the fifth day of the week to receive the tablets of the Law, and descended on the second day. If anyone compares this with the most celebrated fasts of the fourth and sixth days <note>(*)</note> that are accustomed to be undertaken each week in the Roman Church, he will discover clear indications of Pharisaism. Wherefore these fasts were never in use in the purer Church. For although they object to us the authority of Tertullian <note>(y)</note>, it has long since been refuted by Rigaltius <note>(z)</note> that "stations" <gloss>fasting days</gloss> do not signify fasts there, but those assemblies instituted for the sake of prayer, to which Petavius himself agrees <note>(a)</note>. Indeed, that which they oppose from Epiphanius and Clement of Alexandria <note>(b)</note> has been learnedly discussed by Dallaeus <note>(c)</note>. It remains, therefore, that we still inquire whether this also came to the Hebrews under the name of a fast, when each person abstained from the eating of meat. And I am not far from asserting that, since in Tractate *Avodah Zarah* <note>(d)</note>, there is a mention of "fasting from fish." For that perverse opinion had already taken root in the minds of many at that time, as if there were no other way to restrain pleasures and curb lust than by avoiding meats. It was entirely different from what Pythagoras taught <note>(e)</note>, who by his symbol, "do not taste of fish," judged that the eating of fish pertains to luxury and superfluous delights. This error was propagated not only among the Montanists and Tatianists <note>(f)</note>, but the Romanists also received it from the Jews by a quasi-hereditary right. Finally, it must not be omitted that which Gabriel Albaspinaeus <note>(g)</note> reports: that it was once the custom that no one would be greeted with a kiss during the time of a fast, which the *Ordo Romanus* and other writers on rites also confirm. For the custom of the Hebrews, which Maimonides <note>(h)</note> explains, is most similar and closely related to this: "They decrease greetings <note>original: "וממעטין בשאילת"</note>..."

The first of these were Chaldean, with Abraham as the inventor, as Philo says, which the Chaldeans, Assyrians, and Phoenicians used; but there are those who say that Rhodomathus first gave letters to the Assyrians. After these, Moses handed down letters to the Jews, perhaps not indeed in these characters which they use today, which they think were invented by Ezra, whom they consider the writer of almost all the books of the Old Testament. Furthermore, some say Linus of Chalcis brought letters from Phoenicia to the Greeks, but Phoenician ones, until Cadmus, the son of Agenor, gave them new letters in another character, numbering sixteen, to which Palamedes added four during the Trojan War. Afterward, Simonides of Ceos added the same number. But a certain man named Mennon first handed down the use of writing to the Egyptians through the likenesses of animals, as one sees on the obelisks, but Mercury first gave them letters—that Mercury, namely, whom Lactantius says was the fifth Mercury, to whom Vulcan, the son of the Nile, succeeded in the kingdom. But the woman Nicostrata, by the surname Carmenta, handed down letters to the Latins. Seven types of letters therefore excelled in antiquity: Hebrew, Greek, Latin, Syrian, Chaldean, Egyptian, and Gothic <note>original: "Geticae"</note>. Regarding these, Crinitus reports that he read these following verses in a very ancient codex:

Moses first inscribed the Hebrew letters,
With a sagacious mind the Phoenicians established the Attic ones,
Which we Latins write, Nicostrata published,
Abraham found the Syrian and the same the Chaldean,
Isis with no less art brought forth the Egyptian,
Galfila produced the Gothic, which we see are the last.

Digest 9.2.27. **MOM.** The Moon is argued for its inconstancy in a miraculous way; for it is sometimes whole, sometimes half, waxing, waning, silent, curved with horns. And for this reason the Doctors are poorly regarded, because they feel, disagree, distinguish, and divide things into a thousand atoms, not without great cost to the readers. And so, just as those conceived under the Moon fall into the falling sickness, as Quintus Serenus is the author, and those who spend a long time under the Moon fall into delirium, and are called "lunatics" by the jurist in Digest 21.1.1.8, so for the most part, those who follow the trifles and empty disputations of the Doctors everywhere fall into total folly, as those which were invented concerning the "extremes from which" and "extremes to which" in Digest 41.3.31. Likewise, those things concerning direct and common words in the treatise on substitutions. These are the inconveniences of the changeable Moon, which, although it ought to dispel the darkness of the night, as you said in the authentication *Ut iudicia*, section 2, column 2, it doubles the greater darkness, even if it has little to do with the matter. I will seem to you to invade the Stoa, to burn down the Academy, to demolish the Peripatetic school, if I disagree with Bartolus or with the common opinion of others. However, I cannot agree with Bartolus, who thinks that a donation was once a named contract, and is even much more so today, nor with the remaining interpreters, who indeed wish it to be named today, but not formerly, but, what you might wonder at, I assert even after Code 8.53.35 that a donation is an unnamed contract.

Bartolus objects to Digest 39.5.1, where in a donation there is no place for repentance; in unnamed contracts there is, Digest 12.4.3. To which it is commonly responded that no unnamed convention that is not reciprocal admits of repentance after tradition, and it is true.

The same Bartolus falsely notes that a donation takes its name from execution and from the thing handed over, by the example of a loan, a bailment, and a deposit, because a donation is a "giving of a gift," Digest 39.5.1. Therefore, he says, unless it is by the thing itself, it does not produce an action, although it had an elegant name. But that a donation existed before tradition is demonstrated by the said Code 8.53.35, "that it not be useless," as is wont to be said about permutation. I prove that it is entirely unnamed by these little reasons: because it has neither its own name, nor its own action. For it lies so wide that it contains a stipulation made without cause, Digest 39.5.1. But it lacks an action, because there is nowhere an action. For what action competes for a donation in the said section 5 of the law *Si quis argentum*, it is called by law. For from the fact that an action is given by law, the donation itself is shown to be weak, Digest 28.2.29, and, like the Moon, it shines with borrowed light, since it lacks its own. For I did not discuss them in such a way as to affirm that some exist, or to prove through adduced arguments that it is likely. On the contrary, I said that I would refrain from writing more about the kind of astronomy that would exist for the inhabitants of Saturn, precisely because most people consider it too absurd for men to live on planets; and therefore, they would say that I was wasting my time investigating what those might observe who do not exist in the nature of things. However, when I named the months of the Saturnians while calculating the period of the Saturnian Moon, I did nothing new or unusual for astronomers, for whom nothing is more common than to imagine that someone exists on the Sun or Moon, and from there observes the motions of the stars. There was no reason for Fabrius to blame me for having proposed this invention about Saturnians there. And even if it were otherwise, I would be neither the first to have put this forward, nor would it be so ridiculous, at least among philosophers, as he thinks. But I shall not digress into these matters beyond my established purpose. The contemplation of the Fabrian System calls me, namely that one by which, after he demolished mine, he trusts that the phenomena around Saturn can be conveniently explained. For those earlier arguments, by which he attempts to order the motion of Saturn itself with new laws, are irrelevant here, and it would not be worth the effort to examine them. I wonder, however, what displeased him in the Tychonic hypothesis, to make him decide to build a new one from its foundations: one which I fear astronomers can hardly grasp, let alone approve.

But neither is that which pertains to the phases of Saturn in any way clearer, and furthermore, it is so far removed from all reason and likelihood that I do not know if it needs to be refuted by me. For whom, I ask, will this pretty invention of four small globes near Saturn deceive, of which two shine with the light of the sun, while the other two do not reflect rays at all, but are by their very nature most obscure? translation:
->XI.<-

The donation of the one who makes a thing welcome, however, is accustomed to fulfilling this lawfully, worthily, and without doubt or excess.

->XII.<-

This is, as Augustine says, what grace intends: because we are not justified through the law, but through grace. For even if the law had not been established for this purpose of justification, then certainly it would not be considered a legate <note>representative</note> except to lead to this purpose.

->XIII.<-

And Jerome: the thing that is a gift is not through this practice. Hence, grace is called "gratuitous."

->XIV.<-

But if this were constituted through this practice, which it is not, then grace would no longer be grace. It would turn judgment into grace, which would never find gratitude.

->XV.<-

Just as they recite twice for this purpose in these lines, the melody of the agreement. Deference to the donor while it is for the sake of the grace bestowed, from which it holds all effect of verification. However, it does not demand certainty for the gift to be obtained from God entirely in the hearts.

Children under parental power, and slaves to whom the free administration of a peculium <note>gloss: a sum of money or property held by a subordinate</note> has been granted, may give the master's money as a loan, as it is in <note>law 28, Digest on pacts</note> or money from the peculium, as it is in <note>law 2, § penultimate, Digest on this title</note> (for in reality the ownership of the items of the peculium belongs to the master or father <note>law 2, Code on paternal power; § 1, 2, Institutes on through which persons property is acquired</note> although children under power or slaves are meanwhile assumed to be owners <note>law 17, Digest on the peculium</note> and their own patrimony is said to be their own <note>law 5, § 3; law 32 in the end, in the beginning; law 52 in the end, in the beginning; law 47, § last, Digest on the peculium; § 10, Institutes on actions</note>), such that the obligation or action is acquired for the master or father. <note>law 2, § penultimate, joined with law 11, § last, Digest on this title</note>

Et licet eam pro certâ atque omninò indubiâ venditare non audeamus, id tamen firmiter nobis habemus persuasum, quod cæteræ opiniones suis itidem, si accuratè examinentur, difficultatibus, iisque nostris fortè & pluribus & gravioribus, laboraturæ sint.

### §. XXI.

Hoc interea notandum superest, quod ab Evangelistis addatur, Christum propinatum istud vinum bibere recusâsse. Quod quamobrem factum sit, adhuc disceptatur. Sunt, qui eum adversatum fuisse Judæorum volunt malitiam, quâ vinum aceto & felle corruperant. Sunt etiam, qui pro venenato eum istud habuisse opinantur. Aliorum hæc est conjectura, quod dicti illius sui memor esse voluerit, se non bibiturum amplius de fructu vitis, usquedum regnum DEI venerit. (fff) Alii denique eo ipso nostrum indicâsse Salvatorem statuunt, brevi quidem se mortis amaritudinem gustaturum, at paulò tamen pòst resurrecturum esse. Quem in sensum quoque cecinit Poëta Sedulius:

-> - - - *Tetigit labiis & ab ore removit,* <-
translation:
we do not say that it was such, nor do we believe it must be touted as so very sweet, and we agree with the <note>Blessed</note> *Calovius*, who argues that those who claim this confuse myrrh-wine with myrrhed wine. We do not deny that the former was pleasant enough and contributed much to the delight of the palate; but that such great sweetness could be attributed to our own <note>the wine intended for Christ</note> as to move the soldiers to drink it up, and thus to neglect so completely the custom used by the Hebrews, I judge to have little appearance of truth. Furthermore, many are accustomed to remark much regarding this explanation of that Prophetic saying, and it is therefore highly doubtful whether it can be conveniently applied to this deed of the soldiers.

(eee) See, among others, the <term>Pugio fidei</term> <gloss>Dagger of Faith</gloss> by Raymundus Martinus, Part III, Dist. III, § 25, et seq.

### §. XX.

We establish that the end which the Jews had proposed to themselves was twofold: one (which you could also call general), that they might observe the custom received among their own people; the other (which was special), that they might harass Christ with the greater torments. Nevertheless, we will leave to each person the judgment of which of the opinions brought forth thus far he wishes to embrace or reject. To us, certainly, this one, which both Casaubon and most of our own people favor, pleases us above the rest. And although we do not dare to tout it as certain and entirely undoubted, we have this firmly persuaded to ourselves, that the other opinions, if they are examined accurately, will labor under their own difficulties likewise, and perhaps more and graver ones than our own.

### §. XXI.

Meanwhile, it remains to be noted that it is added by the Evangelists that Christ refused to drink the wine offered to him. Why this was done is still debated. There are those who maintain that he opposed the malice of the Jews, with which they had corrupted the wine with vinegar and gall. There are also those who think that he deemed it to be poisoned. The conjecture of others is that he wished to be mindful of that saying of his, that he would no longer drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of GOD should come (fff). Finally, others establish that by this very act our Savior indicated that he would indeed taste the bitterness of death for a short time, but would rise again a little later. In which sense the poet Sedulius also sang:

-> - - - *He touched it with his lips and removed it from his mouth,* <-

he is mortal, but being freed, he conceives a confidence in future immortality. And speaking to *Asclepius*, he says:
<margin>Inventor of medicine.</margin>
> Your grandfather, O Asclepius, was the first inventor of medicine, to whom a temple is consecrated on the mountain of Libya, near the shore of the crocodiles, in which his worldly man lies, that is, his body; for the remainder, or rather the whole—if a man is whole in mind—the better part of life, has returned to heaven.

What can be said more clearly, what more solidly to establish the immortality of the soul? It is evident, therefore, from the very true theology of *Mercury*, that *the human soul is immortal, and that man, not without the great counsel of the Creator, consists of a dual nature.* The text follows.
<margin>The text is explained.</margin>
For he is immortal, as it has been said, and he possesses the will of all things: *both because they are subject to his authority, and also because he can have knowledge of all things.* But other living beings, which are mortal, suffer by being subject to fate, because they serve the course of the stars
<margin>Fate.</margin>
and have no faculty of free will: for the wise man dominates the stars. I have spoken more broadly
<margin>The wise man dominates the stars.</margin>
*on fate in the 4th Pymander.* Man is therefore superior to harmony: that is, the soul, which is of a more divine order, having fallen into harmony, namely the lower one, that is, into the body, having been endangered, has been made a servant: for all danger stems from the bond of matter, and all trouble of unjust servitude stems from the commerce of the body. Here, fortified by the fecundity of both sexes, that is, endowed with the fecundity and abundance of procreating offspring, by Him who is the fountain of both sexes, that is, by God—as he had said a little earlier that God is most full of the fecundity of both sexes: which he certainly elucidates most openly in the *Asclepius*:
<margin>What both sexes signify in God.</margin>
> God, he says, is the only one like all things: most full of the fecundity of both sexes, always pregnant with His own will: He always brings forth whatever He wills to procreate in God: His will is all goodness: this same goodness of all things is born from the nature of His divinity, so that all things may be as they are and have been, and that nature may suffice from itself for all things that will be born hereafter: this is the reason how all things of both sexes come to be.

<margin>The good of fecundity.</margin>
For it is impossible for any of the animals that exist to be unfecund. Since, therefore, God is most full of the fecundity of both sexes—partly, because *His intellect and will are fecund, as I said in the beginning of the second Pymander;* partly also because He provides fecundity for others to bring forth and procreate—it behooves each of us to be fecund not so much in offspring as in virtues: for by this fecundity of both sexes, anyone ought to be fortified, namely, both with the charity of the will and the truth of the intellect; for the offspring of the will is love: but of the intellect, it is truth: and he was made watchful
<margin>The text is explained.</margin>
by Him who is watchful, he is contained and subjected to His dominion. Indeed, not only was man gifted with the bounty of fecundity by his Creator, but also with the grace of being watchful by Him who constantly keeps watch over His works:
> For He does not sleep, nor does He slumber, who guards Israel:

<margin>Man ought to be watchful.</margin>
For it is in man’s interest to be vigilant, lest, burdened by ignorance or the sleep of sloth, he lose himself and his own, which have been granted to him from heaven. He ought to clearly understand how he was created by God, and how he received many things from Him, to whose dominion he is subject, both by nature and by the gifts of grace; and therefore he must be very watchful, so that he may be pleasing and dear to Him under whose dominion he is contained.

They said Muhammad is the brilliant, the equitable,

The Prophet, O Muslims, know with certain knowledge,
That the Lord of the Worlds commanded that we pray upon him.
The Prophet is that beautiful one, his speech is true speech,
And the Quran is a beautiful thing which was sent down upon him.

REVIEWS 311

J. Mazurek. Wydnie szdste, opracowat i uzupeinit Tadensz Radlinski.
Warsaw: Gebethner i Wolff. 1926.

Powszechny Atlas Geograficzny.— Eugenjusz Romer. Lwow-Warsaw:
Ksiaznica-Atlas. 1925. 12 xX 8.

Atlas Statystyczny Polski— Dr. J. Weinfeld, E. Szturm de Sztrem, i Dr.
J. Piekatkiewicz. Warsaw-Bromberg: Instytut Wydawniczy “ Bibljoteka
Polska.” 1925. 14 X I0.

The first of these atlases was originally published in parts, beginning in
1922, and appeared as a complete work in 1925. It has obviously been designed
for a school course involving a careful study of the geography of Poland, other
parts of Europe in less detail, and the rest of the world in outline. The section
dealing with Poland will undoubtedly constitute its chief attraction for non-
Polish geographers, because in addition to the general maps of that country,
and inset maps of all its chief towns, there are folded sheets containing no
fewer than twenty-four small maps dealing with almost every subject of geographical interest—morphology, climate, economic conditions, race, religion,
etc. The whole work is beautifully executed, and a study of it leaves a most
favourable impression of the possibilities of Polish cartography. The representation of the physical geography of Poland is particularly good, and in many
of the distribution maps the choice of colours is admirable. One criticism
must, however, be made, and it is a serious one. The maps are in most cases
too small (the scales vary from 1/3 M to 1/300 M), and the lettering is so fine
that even for a person with fairly good eyesight a. reading-glass is essential.

The second atlas in the above list is a translation of a German school atlas
which was originally compiled by F. Heiderich and W. Schmidt and translated
into Polish. It has since been amplified by T. Radlinski and is now in its sixth
edition. The maps, which have been produced by Hetzee in Vienna, number
forty-five ; of these about half are devoted to Europe, and the remainder are
divided in almost equal proportions between the other continents and the world
asa whole. There are numerous inset maps, some of which, at least, are of
interest. The atlas will, no doubt, prove useful to Polish students, but the
technique shown in its production is not of a high order, and the work as a
whole is inferior to the best German school atlases.

Romer’s atlas, too, is not altogether satisfactory. A few astronomical
diagrams, some charts of the world showing various distributions, several maps
of Poland, and physical and political maps of the continents, constitute the
bulk of the work. The maps of Poland are fairly good, but in general the
draughtsmanship and lithography are not up to the standard of the work
first noticed.

The Statistical Atlas of Poland, of which as yet only two parts have been
received, has as its object a comprehensive survey of the political and economic
activities of the people of that country. It contains much useful information
on a great variety of subjects—for example, population, education, utilization
of the land, mining, banking, language, and religion—and its value is enhanced
by a comparison with the state of affairs in 1913 on the one hand, and with
contemporary conditions in the chief European countries on the other. Most
of the information, it must be admitted, is given in the letterpress ; the maps
are not very illuminating, and consist in the main of circular and rectangular
diagrams placed within the provincial frontiers and indicating for each subject
dealt with the proportion for the province of the total for the whole state.

J. McF.

II. Optimates in Aristocratia et πλούσιοι in oligarchia Aristotelis 4. Politicorum 4. Qui idem juris habent ad successores obligandos, sive in aliam plane formam transitus fiat, sive tempore procedente Imperantes in fata concesserint, vel alia quacunque de causa ordine fuerint moti, sicque alii atque alii in locum priorum surrogati; modo in eo quod gestum est, nullum sit vitium, cum in re ipsa, tum in modo; vel quod non omnibus, vel quod non pluribus gestum fuerit comprobatum, vel alias ubi vota paria sunt, res forte non decisa. vide Magnificum Dominum Boeclerum de calculo Minervae; et alios plures, qui haec ad hypothesin transferentes in mixtura Reipublicae Romanae Germanicae occasione articuli 5. Instrumenti Pacis Paragrapho 19. aliquot distinctionibus magnas controversias in capite de comitiis Imperii componere satagunt.

Prout autem imperantes formae corruptae hic in communionem hujus juris admittimus, ita et in Regno dominatum et Tyrannidem omnino volumus intellectam. Grotius libro 2. caput 14. de Iure Belli et Pacis de his ita loquitur: Contractibus vero eorum, qui sine jure imperium invaserunt, non tenebuntur populi aut veri Reges. libro 1. caput 4. Paragrapho 15. adjicit: nisi pacto vel longa possessione jus imperii fuerint nacti.

Quas adjectiones lubentes admittimus; attamen videbatur posse tentari, istiusmodi invasorem, etiam citra pactum, vel longam possessionem, simulac populus, cujus gubernacula rapuit, arma deposuit, et in defensione juris sui non amplius est constitutus, statim omnia jura in se transtulisse; adeo ut non tantum ejus acta cum aliis rata habenda sint, verum etiam, ut ipse populus omni in istiusmodi invasorem vi destituatur, et ejus acta tanquam auspicio regio gesta suspicere teneatur. vide Magnificum Dominum Boeclerum in dissertatione Grotiana 1. de eo quod civitas egit. pagina 49. Fredericus Horn de civitate libro 2. caput 1. et caput 9. scripta, quae a Dominis Anglis et Batavis, nominatim Miltono et Salmasio, qui priori se opposuit, quo effectu, refert Magnificus Dominum Boeclerum in Musaeo, super hac quaestione typis sunt evulgata.

Next to Kings are the Electors in our Empire, and other estates that rule alone, on account of territorial superiority, concerning which see Wehner in his practical observations under the term <term>Lands-Fürstliche Obrigkeit</term> <gloss>Princely territorial authority</gloss>. Ludolphus Hugo in his treatise on the status of German Regions, chapter 3.

II. The Optimates in an Aristocracy and the <term>plousioi</term> <gloss>wealthy</gloss> in the oligarchy of Aristotle’s *Politics*, book 4. These possess the same right to bind successors, whether a transition is made into a completely different form, or whether the rulers have passed away in the course of time, or for any other reason have been moved from their order, and thus others have been substituted in the place of the former; provided that in what has been done, there is no defect, both in the matter itself and in the manner; or that it was not approved by all, or not by the majority, or otherwise where votes are equal and the matter was perhaps not decided. See the Magnificent Lord Boecler on the <term>calculus Minervae</term> <gloss>the vote of Athena/the deciding vote</gloss>, and many others who, transferring these things to a hypothesis in the mixture of the Roman-German Republic, on the occasion of article 5 of the Instrument of Peace, paragraph 19, strive to settle great controversies in the chapter concerning the assemblies of the Empire with a few distinctions.

However, just as we admit the corrupted forms of rulers into the communion of this right here, so too in the Kingdom we wish for domination and Tyranny to be understood entirely. Grotius, book 2, chapter 14 of *The Law of War and Peace*, speaks of these as follows: "The people or true Kings shall not be bound by the contracts of those who have invaded power without right." In book 1, chapter 4, paragraph 15, he adds: "unless they have obtained the right of rule by pact or long possession."

We willingly admit these additions; yet it seemed possible to attempt that such an invader, even without a pact or long possession, as soon as the people whose reins he seized have laid down their arms and are no longer constituted in the defense of their own right, has immediately transferred all rights unto himself; so that not only should his acts with others be held as ratified, but also that the people themselves are stripped of all force against such an invader, and are bound to look upon his acts as if they were performed under royal auspices. See the Magnificent Lord Boecler in his first Grotian dissertation on what the city has done, page 49. Fredericus Horn on the city, book 2, chapter 1, and chapter 9, writings which were published in print on this question, with what effect, the Magnificent Lord Boecler reports in his *Musaeum*, concerning the English and Dutch Lords, namely Milton and Salmasius, who opposed the former.

Two primary considerations present themselves from this chapter: one concerning wounding, and the other concerning fire. The estimation proper to it, however, must be deferred to the differences between the two chapters, which are held below in Thesis 31. As regards wounds, they are either inflicted by one person or by several. If by one, it is a matter of settled law and beyond all controversy that he is held in solidum. If by several, then with no mortal wound existing, the obligation of all is equal. This is also true if, among other wounds, at least one inflicted by the same attack is mortal, and it cannot be certainly determined among the attackers who made it; law 11, paragraphs 2 and 4, of the Digest under this title, also in the case where it was clearly certain that not all had inflicted mortal wounds; law 51, paragraph 1, and the following of the Digest under this title, by the argument of law 6, of the Digest on arbitrations of theft cases. <header>MISSION TILHO.</header>

Au fond de quelques ouadis, émergent des calcaires argileux blancs, en blocs hauts de un à deux mètres et longs de quatre à six mètres.
10h 10 soir, campé.

15 mai. — 4h 40 matin, en route. Traversé plusieurs cuvettes restreintes, à des altitudes variables, donnant l'impression d'un steppe ondulé.
6h matin, passé à Bou Foumin sans s'arrêter. Le puits ayant été restauré quelques jours avant, les guides peuvent se procurer un peu d'eau. Profondeur du puits, 8 brasses (13 mètres environ). Bou Foumin est l'appellation arabe; les Tédas disent Kollori (Killori de Nachtigal). Après Bou Foumin, on entre dans le Manga.
7h 35 matin, halte dans un bon pâturage d'askanit. Les chameaux, qui n'ont pas rencontré cette plante depuis l'Azbin, s'en régalent.
2h 50 soir, en route. Trois kilomètres après la halte, les ouadis cessent; on fait route sur un plateau sans relief sensible, à l'altitude du sommet des dunes précédentes. La végétation herbacée diminue progressivement. A 20 kilomètres environ vers l'Ouest, aperçu une ligne de hautes dunes s'éloignant vers le Nord-Ouest.
Rencontré deux troupeaux d'antilopes mohor (*euryx leucoryx*).
10h 24 soir, campé. Rares touffes d'herbe.

16 mai. — 4h 04 matin, en route. La végétation herbacée diminue de plus en plus et bientôt on ne trouve que quelques rares pieds de bou rekkeba (mrokba) et de shep (?)<note>(1)</note>.
Très espacés : des talhas, des sarahs (serrahs), du r'tem, souvent sec.
Le sol est de sable à petits grains de gravier.
Très faibles ondulations du terrain, normales à la direction générale de la route. 6h 26 matin, les guides signalent qu'on arrive à la limite de la végétation arbustive. Comme on n'aperçoit d'herbe nulle part, halte pour faire manger les chameaux. Tout le long de l'étape précédente, petites rides de sable normales à la direction générale des vents (E. N. E. et E. q. N. E.).
Nombreuses traces d'antilopes; très peu de gibier en vue.
2h 49 soir, en route. Les arbres se font plus rares : quelques toumdoubs (*capparis sodada*), des sarahs, peu de talhas; herbes par touffes.
Terrain légèrement ondulé normalement à la direction générale de la route. 3h 53, apparition du hâd.
A partir de 5h environ, le sol est couvert de petits monticules de sable élevés par le vent à l'abri de chaque arbuste ou de chaque touffe d'herbe.
9h 27, campé en un point à peu près entièrement privé de végétation.

<note>(1) Cette plante n'a pu être identifiée.</note>

<meta>continues from previous page: ...as they were, and since this custom of the reading was established in Babylon to break the power of the <term>kelipot</term> <gloss>impure forces</gloss>, it was done there in a loud voice, and this practice has been passed down to us.</meta>

The beginning of the service is in the heart, and this is the aspect of <term>bittul ha-yesh</term> <gloss>the nullification of the self/the ego</gloss>, and so on. This matter is very deep, and one must understand how <term>bittul ha-yesh</term> is possible within the heart, for the heart is full of desires and wills. How can the self be nullified within the heart? 

The matter is as it is written: "I have hidden Your word in my heart" <note>Psalm 119:11</note>, and the heart is the dwelling place of the soul. The soul consists of the aspects of <term>Chokhmah</term> <gloss>Wisdom</gloss>, <term>Binah</term> <gloss>Understanding</gloss>, and <term>Da'at</term> <gloss>Knowledge</gloss>. When a person contemplates the greatness of God, the "self" that is in the heart is nullified, and this is the aspect of <term>bittul ha-yesh</term>. This is the aspect of the expansion of the soul into the heart. When the soul expands into the heart, the heart is nullified before God, and this is the aspect of <term>bittul ha-yesh</term>. 

This matter is the aspect of the "service of the heart." The service of the heart is the aspect of prayer. In prayer, a person prays to God and asks for mercy, and this is the aspect of the service of the heart. This is the aspect of <term>bittul ha-yesh</term>. When a person prays, he is nullified before God, and this is the aspect of <term>bittul ha-yesh</term>. 

<summary>This page explores the concept of "service of the heart" through the lens of self-nullification (bittul ha-yesh), explaining how contemplating divine greatness allows the soul to transcend worldly desires during prayer.</summary>

From such alphabets, some take the initial letters of things as their hieroglyphic notes, especially those enunciated in Chaldean or Hebrew. Some transfer wonderful signs and <term>altrilogical</term> <gloss>allegorical/other-speaking</gloss> figures from the Cabala, about which it is superfluous to argue further, especially since nothing can be drawn so ineptly that one could not induce some color to it from geometry and lead it to some figure among the elements of languages. For the present, there appears to us no reason why we should defer to the Chemical monad. And so, we do not dislike the industry of those who fashion the characters of essences from whole hieroglyphic notes of infinite kinds, so that it is clearly manifest, provided one is knowledgeable of the original writing, that it is something artificially produced from them, just as the indices of sublimated and precipitated mercury teach. Thus, if one wanted to designate the crocus of Mars and the flower extracted from it, one could form this image: ♁, to indicate the magisterial crocus; as for the flower, this: ♁, or ♁. White lead in the magistery should be sculpted from the character of Saturn, namely ♄, so that the dots might insinuate calcination. A flower thus: ♄. Dorneiferus poorly observed the foundation when he painted it ♄. If the letter Zeta expressed by the Indian figure of the ternary was meant to designate white lead, the added mark is nevertheless of no art. Because Spanish white is made from white lead through corrosion and reverberatory calcination, it rightfully claims the wood of its matter for itself, and can be painted in its own form ♄. Verdigris is poorly drawn thus ♁: rather so ♁. For it is from Venus and contains her vitriol, and the index of corrosion is different. The common people have expressed litharge in some way from the character of Saturn ♄ or ♄, as if it were an inverted and changed Saturn. It is therefore not correctly adapted to antimony. Indeed, we can use these inversions in designating the liquors of calces, with the mark of water added; so the liquor of lead will be written thus ♄ so that we understand that calcined Saturn has flowed down into water by deliquescence: but oil is different, namely in this manner ♄. For oil is made from liquor by inclination. Other things that are ingenious, people will easily devise from the example of these. They use another principle who adapt the initial letters of the thing to signify the essence or magistery, or add the initial of these to the figure: as CE for to coagulate: FE for to fix. ♁ calx of vitriol. ♁ to distill: ♁ to sublime. Some paint the things from which the metaphor is drawn, or the vessel commonly called a <term>conceptaculum</term> <gloss>receptacle</gloss>, such as: ♁ dead head: ♁ for water of life: or they throw letters into a scheme, which the Hebrews, Chaldeans, Indians, etc., perform more successfully, as ♁ Spirit of wine, who would have written *Brantewein*. ### CHAP. VII.
### On strengthening, repairing, and obstructing vessels.

<margin>To ch. 3, b. 1 of Alchemy.</margin> We could have added the strengthenings, cements, lids, and the rest to their instruments and vessels. But because artisans, partly by whim, luxuriate in the variety and singularity of special instruments and not rarely show their ingenuity, knowledge, and proprietorship in this way: and partly because the nature of circumstances imposes upon them a certain necessity, so that they are forced to invent something on the spur of the moment in which to perfect the magistery: while some do not even place their work in a multitude of vessels; nay, are accustomed to destroy and dismantle their built furnaces and remove their instruments from sight in moments, so that you can hardly detect the traces of the artisan in the place of elaboration: we have judged it more consultative to throw into one chapter those things which might be found concerning this matter in the commentaries that were at hand, and which we have also approved by our own judgment and experience. From there, let each person take what is convenient for him. Here also, that saying holds: *clearer and more unlearned*. <note>A reference to keeping methods simple.</note> Let him who does not wish to hear about clay depart from this workshop. Certain instruments and vessels must be strengthened with a kind of <term>ichneumonian</term> <gloss>predatory/cunning</gloss> art, or a salamandrine one, against the force of fires and the violence of spirits, and induced and encrusted as if with armor, which also protects against external injuries of collision; indeed, in the weakness of matter in great fires, flight, and melting, hope is often in the crust and external armor, even though metal refiners experience that iron and copper instruments easily escape the force of fires by the protection of clay, as can be seen in the nozzles of bellows and their casings. The Chemist smears with clay, or has vessels—glass, cucurbits, phials, and receptor ampullas—smeared, not only around the bottoms, but also the necks, arms, and nozzles, if a greater force of fire is to be applied, as in the reverberatory furnace, in calcinations, or in gentler distillations, although we are not accustomed to use this material easily even in hot ones, as it is made safe from waters like gypsum. Often a circumspect master uses a bare vessel, which an inexperienced person would not dare to attempt. Truly, it is fitting to know the nature of Vulcan and to do nothing precipitately. We sometimes encrust with clay even dishes and shells to the very bottom, in which we dissolve, coagulate, or dry and color something over the coals. Unless earthen vessels transmit moisture and are made of weak clay, or not sufficiently baked and hardened by the potter's hand, we arm and solidify them with the same care. For this reason, we apply it to both furnaces and crucibles inside and out, as the necessity of the work requires. The same happens also to iron ones that are about to endure a stronger fire. For iron is easily calcined and is even weakened by the strong spirits of fumes. Thus, iron furnaces are encrusted; cement boxes, channels, lids; even the ceilings, beams, and pedestals of that material. Sometimes we smear spoons, casting ladles, and tongs inside and out. But it is enough of a lecture if one knows these things should be referred to the weakness of the matter, the length or vehemence of the fires, and external injuries from <term>antiperistasis</term> <gloss>the resistance of a quality by its opposite</gloss>, collisions, etc. Also, a more convenient handling should be referred to, if only we wish to—

### De hoc nomine Ludicrum. Cap. III.

Ludicra (inquit Priscianus) et non ludicria, ab hoc ludicri dicimus. Vergil. in XII. **Neque enim leuia, aut ludicra petuntur praemia.** Per quod uult ludicra tertiae declinationis, cum contra notum sit secundae esse, ut in lege illa frequenter repetita: **Qui artem ludicram exercuerit, in quatuordecim ordinibus primus ne sedeat.** Ars ludicra, est ars histrionica et scenica, et (ut sentio) quicquid nomine ludicri intelligitur. Nam ludicrum, quod est substantiuum, non modo ludus histrionicus est, et scenicus, sed quodcunque lusorium opus, ac ioculare, etiam ludi publici.

### De hoc nomine Ficus. Cap. IIII.

Ficus (idem inquit) etiam uitium corporis quartae est. Martialis primo epigrammatum.
> Cum dixi ficus, rides quasi barbara uerba,
> Et dici ficos Caeciliane iubes.
> Dicemus ficus, quas scimus in arbore nasci,
> Dicemus ficos Caeciliane tuos.

Ex quo ostendit et uitium, et fructum quartae esse declinationis, genere autem differre. Ego uero reperio ancipitem apud Martialem scripturam, et frequentius sic, ut et ipse puto scribendum.
> Cum dixi ficos, rides quasi barbara uerba.
> Et dici ficus Caeciliane iubes.
> Dicemus ficos, quas scimus in arbore nasci,
> Dicemus ficus Caeciliane tuos.

Ante omnia, cur ille risisset Martialem, quod diceret ficus? An non reperitur ficus, saltem pro arbore, atque etiam pro fructu in numero singulari? Non hoc ergo ille ridebat. Quid ergo? quod genere abuteretur? ne hoc quidem. Quippe cum dico ficus, quo genere utar, nemo intelligit. Certe ridebat, quod alia declinatione uteretur, quam ea, qua debebat, ut ex secundo uersu, in quo mutata est declinatio, apparet. Quod si igitur Caecilianus de declinatione agebat, non de genere, debuerat Martialis ad declinationem, non ad genus respondere, ut est putandum: atque adeo necesse est eum respondisse. siquidem (ut ostendi) ille reprehenderat, quod hic ficos diceret, non ficus. Quae reprehensio si uera est, ut Prisciano uidetur, qui uult ficus magis esse quartae, quae unde modestia poetae fuisset, eum, qui recte admoneat, tam execrabili,

### XXXV.

Extrinsically, those of this place are: 1. *Analogs*; thus artificial composites of a different genus, and others joined by apposition and confusion, correspond to a perfectly mixed body in a certain proportion. E.g., buildings, clothing, foods, drinks, medicines, variously gathered and arranged among themselves. A sublime analog of attribution is the glorious body; but the lowest is the damned one. 2. *Opposites*, also to be heeded, some of which relate *relatively*, like mixables. Some *privatively*, like a dissolved or corrupted body. Some *contrarily*, which evidently, by reason of temperament and other qualities, are adverse to a certain mixture in a certain species; of such kind are bodies that are too intemperate, e.g., too warm for man, like *euphorbium* and *pepper*. Or colder than is proper, like the *torpedo* <gloss>electric ray fish</gloss> and *lead*. Or sharp and corrosive, like *orpiment* and *arsenic*. Finally, also, a body is opposed to a body *antipathically*, with the destruction of one or the other induced; thus poisons are internecine <gloss>deadly</gloss> to animate things. *Gradually*, an imperfectly mixed body is opposed to a perfect one, as much by reason of imperfect union, as are *meteors*; as in regard to mixables, when one or another of these is lacking; thus *Crystal*, which seems to consist only of water, is an imperfectly mixed body. *But let us withdraw the hand from*

## To Bertrandus Eygua, Royal Advocate in the Senate of Toulouse.

Prince, as a patron, O Eygua, patron of the prince,
Tullius <note>Cicero</note> can be mute before you.
While timid eloquence presses the golden fountains,
The impious crowd fears you, the pious crowd reveres you.

## To Cupid.

Clytia recalls the absent one and drives away the one following,
Thus, little Cupid, you drag us here and there.
Tantalus is deluded, thirsty, in the midst of waters.
Thirst always holds me as I am carried in the midst.

## To Franciscus Bertrandus, the fourth President of Toulouse.

Worshipper of sacred laws, most holy president,
Who sing learned poems with a tuneful lyre:
You, I confess, happy, shine with clear honor,
But these things are lesser than your genius.

## Epitaph of the Divine Franciscus, King of the Gauls.

Mars, Phoebus, and Pallas have set up a tomb for the king,
With whom law, poetry, and strong arms lie.

## Epitaph of Nicolaus Bertrandus, the fourth President. To Death.

Death, I see the deed, wretched one, concerning you.
It is not right to deny the penalties for wickedness,
When there is more of reason than in a horse.
You take away, not men, but choice pearls,
Kings, then leaders, and the learned:
And you cast your hands into the holy Senate.
If a limit is not provided for these funerals,
You will be guilty of diminished majesty.
You laugh, I guess what you yourself feel:
You do not fear eternal judgment.

## To Antonius Broullatus Moniayus.

You derive your lineage from an illustrious stem,
Yet you prepare to join sacred laws to your family.
Thus, Broullatus, the glory of a double name adorns you:
What you take from your ancestors, what you beget yourself.

(66) For it can perform the role of one ancient Greek exemplar. However, it cannot prejudice the consensus of many exemplars. For we do not want this, that those things which agree with it should be immediately accepted, but those which are dissonant should be repudiated and rejected. In it, in the genealogy of Christ in Luke chapter III, v. 36, Cainan is inserted, whom, however—just as he finds no place in Moses—so we also believe he does not belong to the text in Luke, along with men who have deserved most clearly of the Church: D. Calov in *Critica Sacra* and Tome I of the *Biblia Illustrata* of the New Testament, page 570, Walther in *Harmonia Biblica*, page 91, and Johannes Elai Terserus, Bishop of Linköping, in *Annotationes ad Genesin*, page 131, who gave proof of this evidently. At the beginning of chapter VIII of John, as said above, the story of the Adulterous Woman is omitted, nor, however, is there any doubt that it is a genuine and Canonical part of the New Testament Scripture, whatever Hugo Grotius and Theodore Beza might contradict. See the dissertation which the most celebrated Scherzer published about that story, or the blessed Walther, *Harmonia Biblica*, page 492 seqq. We congratulate ourselves, however, that the Clause of the Lord's Prayer (which the Latin Vulgate edition does not acknowledge, and Robert Bellarmine and Maldonatus contend was added and inserted into the Evangelical text by the Greeks) exists in this version at Matthew VI, verse 13. Likewise, that the word *Jeremiah* is read in it at Matthew chapter XXVII, verse 9, which D. Georgius Calixtus, in *Concordia Evangelistarum* book VI, chapter 11, and in his literal exposition of the Acts of the Apostles at chapter VII, v. 14, judges to have been inserted into the text from the margin by some unskilled scribe, along with certain Calvinists and Roman Catholics. For hence it becomes manifest that these things existed in the most ancient Greek codices, otherwise Ulphilas would not have brought them into his version, and thus not a little weight is reconciled to the commonly accepted reading.

Yet such a thing is not to be deemed alien to humanity, since Holy Scripture also wills *that the corpses of the impious remain unburied, whereby the memory after death is damned. §. 12. Infants and the insane are also deservedly excepted. As regards infants, they lack all distinct judgment of good and evil; they do what they seem to be delinquent in ignorantly and against their will. Finally, they lack choice, and thus are immune from all guilt. But with guilt denied, punishment is also denied. For the *form* of that which is inflicted upon someone, which has the rationale of punishment, is guilt, which is contracted by the transgression of the law. If this is not present, punishment also has no place. Hence Prudentius, *Peristephanon*, Hymn X: *Nor was it becoming to inflict force upon such small innocence by law, etc.* The words of AMESIUS, *On Conscience, book 5, chapter 3, number 8*, bear on this: *A just punishment, he says, in its formal rationale, has respect to antecedent guilt, as an effect to its compelling or meritorious cause. As an adjunct to its similar rule from which it has measure, as a corrective act to its object to be corrected: therefore, it can have no place where no guilt has preceded.* And the Most Excellent Lord Röhrensee, Public Professor of Morals, to be honored in his teaching, in the *Disputation on the Punishment of the Innocent*, says: *There is a necessary and inseparable nexus between punishment, liability, and guilt, such as between antecedent and consequent, that with the consequent given, it is necessary that the antecedent also be given, even if the reverse does not hold.* From these things, therefore, it is most firmly concluded that infants ought to be exempted from all punishment. Wherefore, pregnant women are also not ordinarily punished, lest something be inflicted upon the innocent fetus, which it was for the mother alone to suffer.

§. 13. As regards the insane, they also lack will, nor do they have a purpose of being delinquent. Now, however, it is asked whether an insane person, who falls into insanity after a committed crime, can be punished? The response is negative: because even then he is treated most miserably by insanity, and he has punishment enough. To the afflicted, a further affliction is not to be added. But if a sound mind returns, and the insane person again becomes wise, I do not see why a punishment for the quality of the crime cannot be imposed upon him as well.

The major is brought forward by <term>syntērēsis</term> <gloss>conscience/preservation of moral principles</gloss>: God does not hear the wicked. Its inventor among the Greeks is said to be Prometheus; Crates Mallotes first brought it to Rome, sent to the Senate by Attalus between the second and third Punic Wars, which was later professed with great arrogance by Palaemon, so much so that he gave his name to the art, and it is called the Palaemonian art of grammar. He was a man so arrogant that he boasted that letters were born with him and would perish with him, and so proud that he held all the most learned men of his time in contempt; he even dared to call M. Varro himself a pig. Yet the Latin grammar itself is so needy and subservient to Greek literature that anyone who does not know it should be immediately cast out from the number of grammarians. Thus, the entire logic of literature or grammar rests only upon the custom of the ancestors and their authority, for whom it was pleasing that a thing be called thus and written thus, and that words be composed and constructed in such and such a way, which they then call speaking well. Hence, grammar boasts that it is the art of speaking correctly, but falsely, since we learn that very thing much better from our mothers or nursemaids than from grammarians. Cornelia, the mother of the Gracchi (who were held to be most eloquent), formed their language. The mother Istrina taught the Greek language to Silem, the son of the king of Scythia, Aripithis. It is known that in many provinces where colonies of foreign nations were introduced, the children born always retained the language of their mothers. Hence, Plato and Quintilian determined so felicitously that a suitable nurse should be chosen for boys. Far be it, therefore, that I should transfer this logic of speaking correctly from those women to the grammarians, who, since they profess nothing but grammar alone, know nothing less. Indeed, Priscian could not learn it even in the entire time of his life, and Didymus is said to have written four—or as others say, six—thousand books about it. In all the aforementioned cases, however, when the question concerns the number of creditors, one should not look so much to their persons as to the sum of the debt itself. Therefore, if there are several debtors to whom one and the same sum is owed, and they are <term>correi</term> <gloss>joint debtors</gloss> with respect to that one debt, they are considered as one debtor only: law 10, *On Pacts*. Thus also, if several guardians of a ward have demanded a debt, they sustain the role of only one person, according to the cited law: Straccha, chapter of the treatise, page 6, number 10; Vander, chapter of the treatise, chapter 6, number 12; Mevius, in the cited place, number 105. <summary>This page details the legal procedures for weighing creditor votes in a moratorium (Inducias), establishing a hierarchy of decision-making based on debt sum, headcount, and judicial authority when disputes occur.</summary>

Likewise, he thinks that the Hebrews, along with the Romanists, place the foundation of the Jubilee in the remission of sins, the guilt of which, as they say in the Schools, is deleted by the authority of the Supreme Pontiff, even if they must pay the penalty for the sin itself either in this life or in purgatory. And in that, certainly, the Hebrews agree by unanimous consent: that wicked deeds and crimes are not committed with impunity, and that everyone pays the penalty for them. But that they are expiated, either through pardon obtained from the Pontiff, or even through the fire of purgatory, that never enters their minds. XLVII. Ego hac in re cum quibusdam R. R. breviter sequentia statuo 1. Partes temporis & durationis continuari immediatè se ipsis. 2. Etiam ubicationes rerum continuarum, ut inter se continuentur, praeter suas entitates, & alias conditiones infrà referendas, nihil intrinsecè requirere, nisi simultaneas durationes. 3. Etiam accidentia symbola, & partes substantiales aliter non continuari nisi per immediatas suarum partium ubicationes simul existentes, modò tres insuper hasce conditiones habeant. 1. Ut sint eiusdem speciei, neque ordinatæ ad constituendum diversa entia per se. Unde non possunt invicem continuari formæ terræ & aquæ, neque diversorum equorum animæ. 2. Ut sint extrema divisibilia in plura rationis eiusdem; ob cuius defectum repugnat continuatio inter duos Angelos, vel duas animas rationales. 3. Ut tales partes non insint diversis entibus per se; & sic repugnat continuari inter se, non solùm elementorum formas, sed etiam materias, quantitates, qualitates, & quæcunque illorum accidentia symbola. Neque enim hæc intelliguntur continua, si ipsorum subiecta tantùm contigua sint.

XLVIII. In continuo vel permanente vel successivo præter partes non datur formaliter ullum indivisibile, neque copulans neque terminans. Ratio est. quia talium indivisibilium non est ulla necessitas. Non ad uniendum? quia partes sufficienter copulantur & uniuntur per ubicationes immediatas, & alias conditiones. Non ad terminandum? Nam sive à Deo realiter, sive à nobis per intellectum auferatur superficies terminativa alicuius tabulæ; illa tabula tam bene erit, & intelligetur finita, atque antè; habebit easdem passiones & usum, quem antè. Ad quid ergo necessaria illa superficies distincta?

XLIX. At quoniam non levis est difficultas, quomodo res incipiant ac desinant, & cur aliquæ quidem intrinsecè, aliæ verò extrinsecè; si in tempore non detur formaliter ullum instans: idcirco ad dubium hocce solvendum, respondemus: Illa incipere ac desinere intrinsecè, quæcunque incipiunt ac desinunt tota simul; incipere verò ac desinere extrinsecè, quæcunque incipiunt ac desinunt per partes, ac successivè.

<header>PHILOSOPHICAL ASSERTIONS.</header>

XLVII. In this matter, I briefly establish the following with certain Reverend Fathers: 1. That the parts of time and duration are continued immediately by themselves. 2. That even the locations of continuous things, in order to be continued among themselves, require nothing intrinsically besides their own entities and other conditions to be mentioned below, except for simultaneous durations. 3. That even symbolic accidents and substantial parts are not continued otherwise than through the immediate, simultaneously existing locations of their parts, provided they have these three additional conditions: 1. That they be of the same species, and not ordered toward constituting diverse entities in themselves. Hence, the forms of earth and water cannot be mutually continued, nor the souls of diverse horses. Because parts are sufficiently coupled and united through immediate locations and other conditions. Not for terminating? For whether a finishing surface of some table is removed really by GOD, or by us through the intellect, that table will be just as well and understood to be finite as it was before; it will have the same properties and use as before. For what, therefore, is that distinct surface necessary? XLIX. But since the difficulty is not light, regarding how things begin and cease, and why some do so intrinsically while others do so extrinsically, if no instant is formally given in time, therefore, to solve this doubt, we respond: those things begin and cease intrinsically which begin and cease all at once; but those things begin and cease extrinsically which begin and cease by parts and successively. with previous admonitions, and with perpetual, and erudite annotations. Three things are read here concerning Monsignor Majella: the first is a Dissertation *De Eusebiana Actorum veterum Martyrum Collectione* <gloss>On the Eusebian Collection of the Acts of the Ancient Martyrs</gloss>; in which Monsignor Majella with much doctrine demonstrates that Eusebius never dreamed of writing about the ancient Martyrs, or of composing the History of their Martyrdom, but only of collecting the Acts, as they were written by others, and of uniting them together, as has been done in our ancient Passionals. On this occasion, he exposes to us the origin and the progress of the fabulous opinion that attributes to Eusebius the formation of such Acts, provided that one knows that the Acts collected by him are not entirely lost. He was born in Naples in the month of March of the year 1669, and there he also ceased to live on the 30th of December 1738. Rome admired him in the Pontificates of Clement XI, Innocent XIII, Benedict XIII, and Clement XII, it being possible to say that there was no thorny affair upon which the uncorrupted counsel of Monsignor Majella was not sought. He worked much, he wrote much; but his writings are for the most part either committed to the flames by himself, or are still found unpublished. His character in a single couplet has been very well painted by Signor Niccolò Capassi:

> *And this wise man lived holily, and lived in the Court;*
> *Not only did he scorn riches, he also scorned genius.*

# TO THE BENEVOLENT READER, GREETINGS.

*A copy of this commentary was sent to Geneva, so that it might undergo the examination of men who are highly esteemed for both their manifold learning and their supreme sharpness of wit, before it was printed. In the meantime, while awaiting their judgment, the author added and changed certain things in his second copy, hoping that this one would be more pleasing to them. But since the premature publication of the book frustrated his hope, he took it poorly. However, he considered it his duty at least to warn readers that if, by chance, any syllogism should not appear to be constructed in mode and figure (as the schools say), they should convert the terms of the propositions. XXXIII. De Tempore Imaginario idem judicamus, quod de spatio Imaginario, scilicet ipsum præter durationes rerum intrinsecas, fundantes di- uersas relationes distantiæ et propinquitatis, re ipsâ nihil esse.

XXXIV. Postremò Duratio alia est creata, alia increata. Increata est propria solius DEI, diciturque Æternitas; et definitur à Boëtio: *Intermi- nabilis vitæ tota simul et perfecta possessio.* Duratio creata alia est temporaria, a- lia perpetua. Temporaria est, quæ et principium habet et finem. Perpetua, quæ saltem finem non habet. Velut duratio Angelorum et Animæ rationalis, quæ et Aevum dicitur, et communiter definitur, *Permanentia rei in esse aliquando ac- cepto interminata.*

### DE QVANTITATE.

XXXV. Quantum describit Aristoteles hîc lib. 5. tex 18. *Quod est divisibile in ea, quæ insunt, quorum utrumque vel unumquodque unum quid, et hoc aliquid aptum est esse.* Id est (ut quidem P. Suarez interpretatur) quorum v- trumque aptum est naturâ suâ per sese, ut unum quoddam totum, ab alijs separatum, manere, et quidem quantum est ex vi quantitatis, eodem modo di- visibile, divisibilitate scilicet Physicâ, et naturali, vi cuius unum Corpus naturaliter expellit aliud, vel partes eius à loco, quem ante occupabant.

XXXVI. Est sententia, ut ait P. Suarez, inter Thomistas satis vul- garis, primarium quantitatis effectum formalem esse distinctionem par- tium integralium; ita ut sine quantitate nec Materia prima, nec ulla alia entitas materialis aliquas partes integrantes habeat. Thomistas ex Nostris secutus est P. Vasquez tom. 3. in 3. p. d. 190. à n. 20. Sed contrà 1. Nam sicuti vnaquæque res per se ipsam est ens, ita per se ipsam est vna, et conse- quenter divisa et distincta à quovis alio. 2. Quia aliàs procedendum foret in infinitum. Nam si vna res est distincta ab aliâ per aliam entitatem tertiam, ergo ab illâ tertiâ debebit iterum distingui per aliam quartam, et sic in infini- tum. 3. Quia Materia supponitur ad quantitatem cum totâ suâ entitate. Ergo non potest accipere partes ab illâ: cùm enim totum nihil aliud sit, quàm omnes partes, quod supponitur cum totâ entitate, debet etiam supponi cum partibus. Non potest ergo primarius effectus formalis quantitatis consistere in distinctio- ne partium.

XXXVII. Sed nec primarius conceptus quantitatis consistit in ratio- ne mensuræ, aut in hoc, quòd sit divisibilis, actione Physicâ et naturali, in par-

XXXIII. Regarding Imaginary Time we judge the same as we do regarding Imaginary space, namely that it is in reality nothing, beyond the intrinsic durations of things which found various relations of distance and nearness.

XXXIV. Finally, duration is either created or uncreated. The uncreated is proper to GOD alone, and is called Eternity; and it is defined by <term>Boethius</term> <gloss>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius, Roman philosopher</gloss>: *The whole, simultaneous, and perfect possession of interminable life.* Created duration is either temporary or perpetual. It is temporary if it has both a beginning and an end. It is perpetual if it at least has no end. Such is the duration of Angels and the rational soul, which is also called <term>Aevum</term> <gloss>the Age or Eon</gloss>, and is commonly defined as: *The uninterrupted permanence of a thing in being once received.*

### ON QUANTITY.

XXXV. <term>Aristotle</term> describes a quantity here in Book 5, text 18: *That which is divisible into those things which are present, of which each one or every one is a certain "one," and this "something" is apt to be.* That is (as Father <term>Suarez</term> indeed interprets) of which each one is apt by its own nature in and of itself, as a certain whole, separated from others, to remain, and indeed, insofar as it is from the force of quantity, divisible in the same way, namely by physical and natural divisibility, by the force of which one Body naturally expels another, or its parts from the place which they previously occupied.

XXXVI. It is an opinion, as Father <term>Suarez</term> says, sufficiently common among the <term>Thomists</term> <gloss>followers of Thomas Aquinas</gloss>, that the primary formal effect of quantity is the distinction of integral parts; so that without quantity neither primary matter nor any other material entity has any integral parts. Father <term>Vasquez</term> <gloss>Gabriel Vázquez, Jesuit theologian</gloss> followed the Thomists among our own in Volume 3, part 3, disputation 190, from number 20. But to the contrary: 1. For just as each thing is a being in and of itself, so it is "one" in and of itself, and consequently divided and distinct from anything else. 2. Because otherwise one would have to proceed to infinity. For if one thing is distinct from another by another third entity, then it must be distinguished from that third by another fourth, and so on to infinity. 3. Because matter is presupposed for quantity with its whole entity. Therefore, it cannot receive parts from it; for since the whole is nothing other than all its parts, that which is presupposed with its whole entity must also be presupposed with its parts. Therefore, the primary formal effect of quantity cannot consist in the distinction of parts.
